#2741. Warriors get demolished by Stephon Castle, Spurs

Friday was always going to be an incredibly difficult game for the Golden State Warriors. They were on the road, taking on a San Antonio Spurs team that had won 10 consecutive games. Just on strength of opponent, it was the hardest game of the year for the Dubs.

And then "hard" turned into "impossible" when Steph Curry was injured during Wednesday's loss to the Houston Rockets. With Curry sidelined, the Warriors were, essentially, without hope in this game.

Still, about once a year the Warriors — like most teams — are good for a shocking upset bid when undermanned. Could this be the night where they're competitive against all odds?

It only took a few possessions for the answer to be an emphatic "no." Steve Kerr opted for a small starting lineup — De'Anthony Melton, Brandin Podziemski, Will Richard, Yaxel Lendeborg, and Draymond Green — hoping to outrun a team that they would be catastrophically undersized against, regardless of who they started.

And boy howdy, that — like everything the team tried — did not work. The opening possessions went exactly the way you would expect: the Warriors could not find an inch of space, while the Spurs broke them down. It felt like a team of seven-footers was playing a team of five-footers … it seemed like every Warriors pass was deflected, and every shot was blocked or contested. In the time it took you to figure out how to get this Prime Video game on your TV, San Antonio had taken a 7-0 lead.

They were getting everything they wanted on offense, using the gravity and playmaking of Victor Wembanyama to fully break down a helpless Warriors defense. Kerr called his first timeout less than three minutes into the game, with the Spurs leading 12-0. That timeout helped Golden State's defense a tiny bit, but it did nothing for their offense. 12-0 became 14-0 became 16-0 became 18-0, the best start to a game in San Antonio's history.

Finally, more than halfway through the quarter, the Warriors — who started the game 0-for-11 from the field — got on the board, when Gui Santos absorbed some contact for a tough and-one.

But even that play was emblematic of the struggles, as Santos missed the free throw, and just a few seconds later, the Spurs converted it into a three.

Santos' bucket did not break any dam. Offense was still borderline impossible for the Dubs to come by, though they finally found a few buckets when Wembanyama took a rest. San Antonio's offense, on the other hand, didn't change at all with their superstar sidelined, as Stephon Castle took it upon him to thoroughly feast on Warriors defenders. That, combined with the Spurs making it rain from deep, led to a 38-14 San Antonio advantage after the first quarter. With no Curry, it was clear that the game was already over.

Golden State played much better defense in the second quarter, and the Spurs' offense got a little discombobulated. But that did nothing for the Warriors' offense, which was still stuck on life support. Every bucket was hard to come by — though LJ Cryer had some nice bursts to give fans something to cheer for — and Golden State could do nothing to cut into the deficit. A bad foul on a De'Aaron Fox three with less than a second remaining punctuated an awful half, and the Spurs went to the locker rooms leading 66-33.

The Warriors opened the third quarter with a pair of threes, and then, for all intents and purposes, they walked off the court and called it a night. San Antonio was taller, longer, stronger, more athletic, faster, and happy to flex all of those advantages in every area of the game. The second half was window dressing, and the Spurs weren't even incentivized to take their foot off the gas, since it was an NBA Cup game, and thus, point differential mattered. The lead ballooned to 43 points for the Spurs, before coming back to an ever-so-slightly less-disrespectful 38 by the final buzzer, with San Antonio winning 123-85.

Cryer was the Warriors' lone bright spot, as he scored a career-high 20 points with six assists (and no turnovers!), while shooting 6-for-11 from three-point range. Charles Bassey, who had 11 points and five rebounds, was the only other Golden State player in double figures.

With Curry out, the Dubs are going to rely on Lendeborg and Podziemski to carry the offense, but neither could do so against the ranginess of San Antonio's excellent defense. Lendeborg had far and away the worst game of his young career, as he shot 1-for-13 from the field for three points, seven rebounds, one assist, and three turnovers. Podz wasn't much better, as he had eight points on 2-for-10 shooting. As a team, the Warriors shot a paltry 33.3% (31-for-93) from the field. The Spurs' length gave the Dubs fits, as they shot significantly worse inside the arc than beyond it … they shot 15-for-41 (36.6%) on threes, but just 16-for-52 (30.8%) on twos, while only earning 11 free throws.

Castle led San Antonio with a brilliant game, finishing with 32 points, five rebounds, and six assists. Wembanyama only played 21 minutes, but that was enough for him to have 12 points, 12 rebounds, six assists, one steal, and two blocks.

The Dubs now get the weekend off, before facing the New Orleans Pelicans on Monday.

#2740. John Harbaugh knew about the Jameis Winston "who let the dogs out?" cadence

Thursday night’s game between the Commanders and the Giants introduced a new wrinkle to the legend of Jameis Winston.

While attempting to get the Washington defense to jump offside on a fourth-and-one play in the fourth quarter, Jameis capped his pre-snap call with, “Who let the dogs out?”

The move invited curiosity as to whether Jameis was simply being Jameis and seizing on the moment, or whether coach John Harbaugh knew that the homage to the Baha Men was part of the plan.

Last night, it’s possible that the specific cadence could have prompted one of the defenders to start laughing loud enough to tumble forward in his stance.

Regardless, it was fun. And that’s when football is at its best — when it’s fun.

#2734. Statcast Check: How Today’s Cardinals Prospects Compare to Walker and Winn at 19

The 2026 Palm Beach Cardinals had five teenage prospects post a wRC+ above 100 while taking 100+ plate appearances: Miguel Hernandez, Sebastian Dos Santos, Yairo Padilla, Ryan Mitchell, and Alexander Frias. That seems pretty good! There were only 14 players total that met these criteria in the ten-team Florida State League.

In 2021, the FSL was loaded with prospects. There were 18 teenagers in the Low-A league to accrue at least 100 plate appearances. The wRC+ leaderboard for that season has some names you will recognize.

Fast-forward to the present day, and the six bolded players have a Steamer-projected wRC+ of 95 or better heading into next year. All except Winn have a projection of 106 or better. From this quick snapshot, I can conclude that the Cardinals should get an MVP candidate and a couple of All-Stars out of their current group of teenage prospects!

2021 was also the first year that Statcast data was publicly available in the FSL. I thought it would be interesting to compare the underlying metrics of the 2021 class with the Cardinals' young guns of today. I do want to emphasize that all the numbers we are looking at are super small sample sizes and groups of players. I am not trying to force conclusions by looking at this data, but I do think it is some interesting context to consider.

Before we get to the comparison with our current Cardinals prospects, let's see if any metrics jump out as being especially important in predicting future success. I separated the 2021 class into two groups, the Hits (Walker, Keith, Winn, Dominguez, De La Cruz, Mesa Jr.) and the Busts (the 12 teenagers who have not made it yet). Here are the average metrics for each bucket.

Not surprisingly, the players who ended up being good were better at 18 and 19 than their counterparts. Masyn Winn was the only player from the "Hit" group to post an average exit velocity below 86.6 mph. In this small sample size, max EV was actually even more important with all six Hits posting max EVs of 109.8 mph or higher. Contact% and Zcontact% were fairly good indicators as well. Chase% was actually better for the Busts thanks to some wild early swinging from a trio of future Hits.

And here is how the Cardinals prospects stacked up.

A couple of disclaimers when looking at the data for the Cardinals prospects. Padilla, Frias, and Hernandez each had fewer than 130 plate appearances, so take their metrics with a spoonful of salt. The other obvious difference is that the 2021 class of Hits only had one 18-year-old while the Cardinals group included three.

Let's run through each Cardinals prospect and see how they compare to the 2021 Hits, Busts, and one just-for-fun comp from the Hit group.

Mitchell's metrics aren't great and fit in comfortably with the Bust cohort. One silver lining is that he was hitting with much more authority earlier in the year before trailing off in July and August (average EV from 87.2 to 81.9). It is reasonable to assume that the grind of his first pro season wore him out in the second half. Hopefully he comes to camp with some added strength. His contact and discipline metrics would look fine for a power hitter, but won't be playable unless he adds some serious pop.

Padilla checked in with only 128 plate appearances, but you can see from his Statcast metrics why the Cardinals are so high on him. The concern with Padilla is that he struggles to hit the ball in the air. His FSL groundball rate was a terrifying 64%. For reference, Jordan Walker was at 55% in his FSL stint. Padilla will be a good test for the Cardinals player development group, but this will require him staying on the field. He has played in only 35, 38, and 27 games the last three seasons.

Frias only had 110 plate appearances with the Cardinals. The comparison to De La Cruz would look better if we had Frias' data from his time with the Brewers. He hit a ball 117 mph while in the complex league and carried a 77.7% contact rate at the Brewers' Low-A affiliate. Frias will, presumably, start 2027 in Palm Beach and hopefully will start bringing more of his prodigious power into game action.

Hernandez blitzed the FSL in his 102 plate appearances to the tune of 163 wRC+. His underlying metrics do not jump off the page, but Hernandez is the youngest player in our cohort (turned 18 on June 2). He was listed at 6'0″ and just 145 pounds when he signed, but Brian Walton at The Cardinal Nation now has him up to 165 pounds. Similar to Dos Santos, how he develops physically will go a long way to determining his ultimate ceiling. It is encouraging to see he has already hit a solid 108.8 mph max EV.

Dos Santos had 255 plate appearances in Low-A, so he has a decent sample size. Not captured in this table is the fact that Dos Santos has an elite ability to drive the ball in the air to his pull side. The Cardinal Nation lists Dos Santos at 6'0″ and 173 pounds, up from his weight at signing of 140 pounds. Dos Santos is a switch hitter and had a bit more success, both from a production and underlying metrics perspective, from the left side.

The Dos Santos/Keith comp is about as close as I am going to get on any of these from a metrics perspective. If Dos Santos can turn into a better defensive version of Keith, that would be a heck of a player. Still, I am holding out hope that Dos Santos can get to another gear in his power as he fills out and matures.

So, what do we need to see next season? All six of the 2021 Hits advanced a level in 2022, and four of the six reached Double-A. Even Dominguez, the lone 18-year-old, repeated Low-A, cleaned up his plate approach, and finished the year in Double-A. The current cadre of Cardinals prospects is young, but to stay on pace with their 2021 forefathers, they will need to advance quickly. I will be watching to see if Mitchell comes to camp with added muscle, if Dos Santos and Hernandez can add a few ticks of EV thump, and if Padilla and Frias can improve their batted-ball quality.

#2726. 49ers to face struggling Cowboys defense, but S.F. has concerns as well

Kyle Shanahan vs. Christian Parker. Folks, this doesn't look like a fair fight.

Shanahan, the San Francisco 49ers head coach, is in his 19th season as an offensive play-caller. Parker, the Dallas Cowboys defensive coordinator, is a rookie in his role.

Shanahan has a coaching tree, assistants who have exited and taken his much-imitated system with them. Parker has a coaching assistant who unexpectedly entered this season to help fix Parker's broken system: Dallas brought Mike Pettine out of retirement last month, making the former NFL head coach and coordinator a defensive assistant.

Remember the 49ers' 38-17 win last weekend over the Raiders and their disastrous defense? Sunday could be the sequel when the 49ers visit the Cowboys, owners of a group that ranks 31st in the NFL in rushing yards allowed, 30th in total yards, 28th in yards per play, 25th in points and, well, there's more, but you get the idea.

The 49ers were asked this week why one of the NFL's worst defenses - statistically speaking - could be friskier than expected.

"We never look at a team's stats," offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said. "We don't let that tell us anything. We watch the tape. This is the NFL and, first of all, every team is well-coached. Every team has good players. And we watch the tape, and we see who's out there."

The tape does show the Cowboys being gashed on the ground. They have allowed three runs of 40-plus yards, an NFL high, and 11 runs of 20-plus yards, tied for the most in the NFL. What Shanahan has told his players: If you take away all the bad plays by the Cowboys defense, they'd be good.

"Coach Shanahan shared with us that - I think they're ranked 31st in run defense - but they've given up (three) 50-yards-plus runs," tight end George Kittle said. "So if you just take off those explosives, they're like a top-12 defense."

In fairness to Parker, he inherited a mess. The Cowboys have allowed 20-plus points in 16 straight games, the longest streak in the franchise's 67-season history and the longest in the NFL since the Jaguars had a 25-game stretch from 2019-2021.

Niners quarterback Brock Purdy, the leader of a 7-1 team with the NFL's sixth-ranked offense, did note the Cowboys (4-5) aren't winless or sackless, tied for 20th in the league with 17 sacks.

"They can make you pay," Purdy said. "They've won games and have gotten quarterbacks in some situations where the quarterbacks had to play ball and be smart."

Trouble in the secondary: Covering Cowboys wide receivers CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens presents a challenge for any NFL team. It becomes especially hard for a team that doesn't have its top two cornerbacks.

Deommodore Lenoir (foot) and Renardo Green (back), who have played 95% and 97% of the 49ers' defensive snaps this season respectively, are questionable for Sunday's contest. Defensive coordinator Raheem Morris said the 49ers will "take it all the way to game day" to see if they can play. It seems more likely than not that they will; both participated in Friday's walkthrough after sitting out practices Wednesday and Thursday.

If one or both can't go, however, the 49ers would turn to rookie cornerback Ephesians Prysock, who has played sparingly, and a combination of Nate Hobbs and Jack Jones. Hobbs (adductor) is not a sure bet to play Sunday - he's questionable and is yet to be activated off the injured list. Jones was cut two weeks ago and re-signed to the 49ers' practice squad this week as extra depth.

Nickel cornerback Upton Stout is also questionable with a shoulder injury.

Lamb put up 195 yards on 10 receptions last Sunday in a win over the Indianapolis Colts. You can't sell out to shut down Lamb, though. When the Tampa Bay Buccaneers did that earlier this season, Pickens feasted with 130 yards on nine catches.

This is San Francisco's biggest concern against a prolific Cowboys passing offense that ranks third in the NFL in total yards.

"You're very confident with your roster and with the guys you have," Morris said. "You're going to give up some yards to these kinds of guys. It's the National Football League."

Pound the rock: The biggest sign of an elite offense is a healthy running game. Hence why the 49ers are 10-0 when they have run the ball 40 or more times during the Shanahan era.

That was Shanahan's goal heading into last Sunday's game against the Raiders - the NFL's worst run defense - and the Niners achieved it. They registered 43 rushing attempts in their win, their first time reaching the threshold since 2023.

Don't be surprised if Shanahan looks to cross that mark again Sunday, with his team facing Dallas' ragged run defense.

To make that a reality, though, the 49ers can't just rely on starting running back Christian McCaffrey, who is an effective player but not the talent he used to be. Even against that porous Raiders run defense, McCaffrey averaged 3.8 yards per carry. His season-long average of 4.5 yards per carry is an improvement from last year's figure (3.9), but the 30-year-old is not breaking off explosive runs at the rate he used to.

Purdy chipped in a season-high 40 rushing yards against Las Vegas. Backup running back Kaelon Black - in just 18 snaps - registered 11 carries for a career-high 70 yards. After a five-week lull where he earned just 67 total snaps, Black has once again emerged as a formidable option.

If the 49ers want to dominate on the ground again Sunday, they'll need to trust their non-McCaffrey weapons. Just like they did last weekend.

Injury concern: The 49ers hope Sunday's game goes better than Thursday's practice. Left tackle Trent Williams suffered a shoulder injury, was unable to practice Friday and is questionable to play against Dallas. Linebacker Dre Greenlaw suffered a knee injury, was limited in Friday's session and is also questionable.

Williams' unavailability on Friday suggests he could be truly iffy. He suffered a shoulder stinger in a Week 3 win against the Cardinals that forced him to exit early. Shanahan indicated Williams' latest shoulder injury was unrelated.

"Anytime you hurt your shoulder on a Thursday, it doesn't make you totally at ease," Shanahan said. "Sunday comes fast, but hopefully that's enough time for him to be all right."

Williams, if he's sidelined, would be replaced by Vederian Lowe, 27. Lowe has played 36 offensive snaps this season after signing a two-year, $9.3 million contract in March.

#2725. Eagles will release WR Hollywood Brown, at his request

#2723. Steelers-Bengals rematch might have the highest stakes of NFL season so far

The Pittsburgh Steelers and Cincinnati Bengals may well decide the AFC North with their Sunday Night Football rematch Nov. 16.

It feels quite early to be making such a bold declaration. Fully nine weeks of action remain starting with NFL Week 10 this week, and they could include plenty of twists and turns that we don't anticipate right now.

On paper, however, soft schedules could make it difficult for the loser of this primetime matchup to make up ground on the other over the course of the next couple of months.

Required reading: Steelers' Omar Khan stands pat at trade deadline, makes no major moves

Both are 6-2 currently, and one will leave the weekend with a full one-game lead. If the Steelers win, they'll also own the head-to-head tiebreaker thanks to their 30-27 victory when these teams first met Sept. 27 at Acrisure Stadium.

Steelers fans originally feared another second-half meatgrinder when dates were announced back in May. Opponents including the Philadelphia Eagles, Denver Broncos, Houston Texans, Jacksonville Jaguars and Carolina Panthers all made the playoffs last season.

The slate also includes both matchups with the division rival Baltimore Ravens, who pushed the Steelers to the final play of the final game of the regular season to decide which team would represent the North in the 2025 playoffs.

Ricky Pearsall, SF (knee) - Out for seasonRicky Pearsall of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026, in Santa Clara, California.

Chris Brazzell, CAR (knee) - Out for seasonChris Brazzell II of the Carolina Panthers warms up during the Carolina Panthers Training Camp at Carolina Panthers Practice Fields on July 23, 2026, in Charlotte, North Carolina.

Jayden Higgins, HOU (knee) - Out for seasonJayden Higgins of the Houston Texans catches a pass for a touchdown during the second quarter of the game against the Indianapolis Colts at NRG Stadium on January 04, 2026, in Houston, Texas.

Ricky Pearsall, SF (knee) - Out for seasonRicky Pearsall of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026, in Santa Clara, California.

Chris Brazzell, CAR (knee) - Out for seasonChris Brazzell II of the Carolina Panthers warms up during the Carolina Panthers Training Camp at Carolina Panthers Practice Fields on July 23, 2026, in Charlotte, North Carolina.

Jayden Higgins, HOU (knee) - Out for seasonJayden Higgins of the Houston Texans catches a pass for a touchdown during the second quarter of the game against the Indianapolis Colts at NRG Stadium on January 04, 2026, in Houston, Texas.

Things look far more manageable now. Of those six opponents, only the Jaguars and Broncos currently have winning records, and the Steelers play only one of the two on the road. They'll travel to face Jacksonville on Monday Night Football on Dec. 14.

The Eagles (2-7), Texans (3-5) and Panthers (3-5) have been among the league's worst teams through nine weeks. The Ravens (4-5) aren't quite as bad, but are navigating injuries to former MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson and his backup Tyler Huntley.

Throw in a Week 17 visit to the 1-7 Tennessee Titans on Jan. 3 and it's reasonable to expect the Steelers will be favored in most of their games the rest of the way.

The road is only slightly tougher for the Bengals. Of their remaining opponents, only the Panthers were a 2025 playoff team.

The Washington Commanders (2-5-1), New Orleans Saints (3-5) and Indianapolis Colts (2-7) all have losing records as well. And one matchup remains against those hobbled Ravens on New Year's Eve.

Cincinnati will face three teams with a winning record compared to Pittsburgh's two. Both division matchups with the 5-3 Cleveland Browns remain, and a Dec. 13 home game against Patrick Mahomes, Travis Kelce and the 6-2 Kansas City Chiefs could be tricky.

Still, the Bengals would have plenty of reason to feel confident if they could pull out a win against the Steelers in a game in which they're currently favored by 3.5 points, per BetMGM.  That reality puts a premium on winning for both sides.

Bigger picture, neither team looks like it's in a ton of danger of missing the playoffs. Eight AFC teams currently have winning records, and seven can make the playoffs. Most of those contenders have tougher remaining schedules, so both the Steelers and Bengals would need to fumble badly to miss the bracket.

The winner of the North gets a coveted home playoff game, though. And that's of particular importance to the Steelers.

They've not won a postseason game since 2016, and they're just 2-6 in playoff road games since their Super Bowl loss to the Green Bay Packers at the end of the 2010 season.

The stakes are therefore fairly high for a game this early in the season.

The Bengals prevailed when these teams last met in Cincinnati early last season. Backup quarterback Joe Flacco sliced and diced the Steelers' secondary for 342 yards and three touchdowns in what became a 33-31 victory Oct. 16.

Otherwise, the Steelers have won in three of their past four visits to Paycor Stadium. The teams have split their 12 meetings, 6-6, since star Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow broke into the league in 2020.

#2722. Lessons in Vanderbilt Football: Mississippi State

The Vanderbilt Commodores ended the looming threat of going winless in the SEC. They breathed a little life back into a season that has fallen below expectations but is still salvageable, even if the likelihood is low. At 4-5 (1-5 SEC), the Commodores really need to win at least 2 of 3 from a home game against #3 Alabama, a trip to newly-unranked Florida, and a rivalry week showdown in Nashville against #8 Tennessee. Of course, for most Vanderbilt fans, a single win to end the season that may knock a rival from the College Football Playoff may be enough to save any season. Realistically, the program needs this team to get to a bowl game for the extra practices as the roster transitions to the next phase and as a better starting point for the career of Jared Curtis.

The win in Starkville looked like it was going to be free and easy at halftime. Vanderbilt had gone on the road and had their second straight 10-0 lead, but, unlike Kentucky who was able to quickly get off the mat in the first half and was up 14-10 at the break, Mississippi State was completely listless through 30 minutes. Then it started to look like the Arkansas and Kentucky script where disasters snowballed. A blown coverage led to a 65-yard TD that doubled the Bulldogs' offensive production to that point. Vanderbilt's ensuing offensive possession ended in a strip sack that was returned for a TD. Suddenly, 16-0 was 16-14, and Vanderbilt went 3 and out to follow.

Thankfully, the defense quickly got back to form and forced a 3-and-out of their own. Brock Taylor made his third Field Goal of the game, a 54-yard effort, and the game mostly settled into a defensive struggle where Vanderbilt held the upper hand. Personally, it feels like a lot of the good things from the Kentucky game showed up again and even stronger against a weaker opponent, but some of the same issues that have plagued the season also made what should have been a blowout into a tight contest.

Brock. Freaking. Taylor. The cannon-legged kicker went 6 for 6 with kicks of 54 and 55 yards as the crown jewels. The longest of which proved to be the game-winner when it gave Vanderbilt an 8-point lead with just 1:46 to go in regulation. Mississippi State would score a TD but fail on the 2-point conversion attempt. The Vanderbilt-record FG kicking performance was 1 make short of tying the NCAA record for a game. It also brought Taylor's career marks to 44 of 50 with the yardage splits as 7/7 from 20-29, 18/19 from 30-39, 11/14 from 40-49, and 8/10 from 50+. The kid has a special leg. It saved Vanderbilt in Starkville.

Tyler Ebel had a decent day but was understandably overshadowed by his kicking partner. The first punt was just barely a touchback that ruined a 54-yard blast by turning it into a net of just 34 yards. His second kick was Brocket Launcher-esque when he blasted it 64 yards over the punt returners head to be downed at the 9-yard line. His next kick was lower and "only" flew 40 yards before bouncing and rolling another 9 yards where it was downed. His "weak" effort for the day was a 39-yard punt that was fair caught. Then the coverage team swamped a frisky returner who went backwards 3 yards to net Ebel 45 yards on a 42-yard punt. In a tight game, having a punter averaging 46.2 yards NET is a big boost. That is how you flip field position and force offenses to go the long route to paydirt.

Not committing back-breaking penalties can lead to success! Vanderbilt was penalized 6 times for a mere 25 yards. The first was a Cade McConnell false start that Jared Curtis immediately erased by hitting Cole Spence up the seam for 20 yards. Carson Lawrence was offside on a kickoff that went for a touchback, so that let State start at the 30 instead of the 25. That drive went 3 and out. The most painful penalty was probably CJ Heard jumping offside to give State a free play on 2nd and 12. The pass, probably a risk taken because of the known penalty, was intercepted, but the worst part was turning 2nd and 12 into 2nd and 7. On 3rd and 7, after no gain on a running play, AJ Swann would hit the 65-yard TD over coverage that might have been even deeper and safer on a 3rd and 12. The second worst was an Illegal Substitution that turned a 4th down with less than a yard to convert into a 4th and 6 FG attempt that was made. Still, it may well have taken 4 points off the board in a moment where Vanderbilt could have gone up 23-14 instead of just 19-14. Then the final two penalties were on back-to-back plays with Ja'Cory Thomas having a 0-yard loss-of-down call for Illegal Touching when he stepped out of bounds before dropping a pass along the sideline then Marcus Veney false starting. Both of those were wiped out by Jamezell Lassiter taking a screen pass for 18 yards and a reset of the chains. It was a pretty clean game where Vanderbilt only really hurt themselves twice, but they still swung potentially 11 points in a 2-point victory.

The other factors in playing clean were almost all smooth. Curtis does need to be more secure with the ball in the pocket or when starting to buy time in the pocket. He has been stripped a few times, and he had another one go for a TD. The other moment was a kickoff going out of bounds, which I guess is not technically a penalty even if they throw a flag? Also, the ESPN box score incorrectly lists it as a Taylor kickoff, not Justin Dewers. I do not understand why we decided to get tricky on the kickoff following the FG to make it 19-14. The Bulldogs were awful on offense. Why give them a free 10 yards? At best you gain 10 to 15 yards, but our offense was also generally moving the ball well until getting across midfield or deeper. It would make sense to try something like that if you get into a track meet where both teams are scoring consistently, and you think that pinning them deeper than the typical 25-yard line starting point may get more conservative playcalls or present an opportunity for forcing a turnover as a returner gets caught out by the funky kickoff.

The offensive line was … below average but not abjectly bad. The OL had a new alignment, too. Lyndon Cooper, Caleb Azubuike, and Cade McConnell kept spots while freshman Mitchell Smith was in at Strong Guard and CJ Williams and Beau Johnson alternated at Strong Tackle. I do not have a snap count split for Williams and Johnson, but the Vanderbilt depth chart for Alabama lists Williams as the starter. A team with 21 sacks entering the game (2.6 per game) had 2 sacks. The Bulldogs did make 9 Tackles for Loss, but they only created 37 yards worth of negative plays. The two sacks accounted for 22 of it, and a Junior Sherrill tap pass was another 5. On rushing plays, Vanderbilt had a total of 10 yards lost over 6 plays. The trio of Sedrick Alexander, Makhilyn Young, and Jamezell Lassiter had 38 carries for 139 yards, which is not impressive but fits in with the game-grinding style akin to the 2024 team (3.83 YPC average for the season even including sacks so still better but similar) that held the ball forever and just wore defenses down in slug fests. Having 39 minutes and 55 seconds of possession fits that mold, too.

Curtis was protected quite a bit in this one. Whether it was a function of coaches deciding to go back to the 2024-style grit-and-grind offense or wanting to protect a young QB behind a shaky offensive line, Vanderbilt's freshman phenom threw just 27 passes two weeks after throwing it 36 times against Kentucky. He was an unspectacular 17 of 27 for 168 yards with no touchdowns or interceptions. He carried the ball 13 times for 22 yards, but he had a long of 22 and was effective other times with the 22 yards in sacks dragging his rushing totals down significantly. One other rushing loss was a pass play that he decided to pull down that was not counted as a sack. The 40.9 QBR is disappointing. He missed a few throws that he should make and needs to make in the future. He has the talent to clean it up. The test he faces today against Alabama is definitely a sink-or-swim moment.

Junior Sherrill was huge again. He had 7 catches but only gained 41 yards. For only the second time all season, he was not the leading receiver in terms of yards. Similarly to the Ole Miss game where Ja'Cory Thomas caught 3 passes for 60 yards, Tristen Brown had 2 catches for 52 yards. Sherrill did have a bad 3rd down drop on a slant that would have given Vanderbilt a first down near the Mississippi State 10-yard line. It was the only notable mistake he made all game.

The depth of options for Curtis had a fair showing. Brown had the aforementioned success while Sedrick Alexander caught 3 passes for 30 yards. Cole Spence and Jamezell Lassiter both had singular receptions for right around 20 yards. Martel High, Jayvontay Conner, and Ja'Cory Thomas also each had 1 catch but gained 3 yards or less. Feeding Sherrill for volume then using others for impact could be a viable strategy, especially with the new gadget on offense.

The misdirection is potentially back to stay. It never should have left. Vanderbilt used jet motion at least 7 times with 4 fakes that were handed off to a RB, 2 tap passes, and 1 fake into a HB screen. I think it was used probably 3 or 4 more times, but I did not necessarily note it every time it happened. The use and execution were not always perfect. I fully support more misdirection to help Curtis identify rushers and make defenders declare their responsibilities pre-snap for you. Maybe Back has more up his sleeves.

The defense was its perfectly inconsistent self. Granted, it is all but impossible to be perfect defensively for an entire game. The defense had 3 drives where they allowed 231 of State's 297 yards of total offense. Allowing 3 scoring drives per game is nothing to be ashamed of. The score looks worse for them because of the defensive TD by the Bulldogs. Vanderbilt's defense only allowed 16 points. Even against an offense struggling like Mississippi State is, allowing only 2 TDs and a FG is going to be a recipe for success. The defensive line was able to create consistent pressure with just 4 rushers. They only sacked Swann 3 times, but they batted at least 2 passes and were in his face preventing him from stepping into throws or making it hard to find targets downfield often.

Two young defenders are really standing out even if the overall unit is doing too much up-and-down. Davin Chandler was listed as a safety to start the year and was at the bottom of the depth chart. He has become a starting cornerback. Players typically move from CB to S as they move from high school to college or college to the NFL and are not up to standards in coverage. I cannot remember any player moving to CB from S, especially not making the dramatic leap from the opening depth chart to the current one. He had 2 fantastic pass breakups by ripping the ball out of WRs hands before they completed the catch. Both were downfield plays that could have totally changed the game. Chandler also had 7 tackles with 5 being solo as he consistently blew up quick throws to the perimeter for limited, if any, gains. His fellow freshman partner in crime is Mason Lewis. Lewis led the team in tackles at State with 10. The good news for a safety is that only 3 were solo. He also defended two passes. These two have deserved more mention here than they have gotten so far.

If Clark wanted an "identity" game, he got it. The game plans from both Beck on offense and Gregory on defense were obvious but executed with commitment and focus. The offense was not always pretty, nor did it score as many TDs as anyone would like, but they ground Mississippi State down to the point that the rushing game ticked up to a 4.0 YPC average for the 4th quarter, which is 0.9 YPC better than the average for the game.

The missed opportunities made life more difficult instead of totally sinking the ship. The penalties that turned a State 2nd and 12 into 2nd and 7 then eventually a 3rd and 7 deep ball TD and an Illegal Substitution that ruined a 4th and very short stand out. The Sherrill drop comes into play here, too. The biggest culprit is Clark Lea. He got too conservative and too "safe" too soon. Being okay with a FG before halftime instead of risking giving the ball back to Mississippi State with very little time left in a half where they awful was so incredibly cowardly. If you believe in your team and want them to have that confident and brash mentality, you have to support it instead of stifling it. That sequence left Mississippi State hanging around. If the score is 20 to 0 going into the break, that game feels a lot safer while looking a lot bleaker for State. Lea should know that stepping on the other team's throat is the best path to victory by now, but he seems to either forget or still does not believe it.

With one win down in the question from last week about a 2016/2018 flourish to finish the regular season and get to a bowl, can Tim Beck match Andy Ludwig's creativity and week-to-week building upon previous success? Especially in 2016, Vanderbilt was pulling out plays fans had never seen before one week then running misdirection, if not outright trick plays, off the new play the next week. The offense went back to basics for Mississippi State with a lot of straight forward zone running plays. They also relied on pre-snap motion a lot but settled into a rhythm of faking to the motion man then handing off to a running back. Unveiling more creative passes, like the HB screen to Lassiter they did pull out in Starkville, from those motions could be lucrative. A key piece to some of that creativity may be a fully converted cornerback.

What is Martel Hight's role and impact now that he has moved to offense full time? The two-way player experiment in 2025 never bore much fruit for the offense. He had 1 carry for 2 yards and 7 catches for 64 yards before it was quashed after Week 3. Hight then went back to full-time defense and punt returner. I do not have a precise Starkville snap count for Hight, but it was probably in the 10-ish play range. He caught a tap pass and was open on a deep crosser that Curtis never saw due to pressure. Curtis did target him down the sideline on a pass that should have been a TD if it had not been left short enough that the DB caught up and had it bounce off his helmet or back. That throw belongs in the "missed opportunities" category, too, since it was on 3rd and 7 from Vanderbilt's own 28 and was followed by a punt. Hight's play at CB has not been up to his usual standards, but this seems like a bad move for him personally. Any future he may have in professional football is surely on defense. I do love his enthusiasm to contribute on offense. I hope it is useful enough to outweigh any downstream impact.

#2716. Giannis, Bam join LeBron, Wade in exclusive Miami Heat club

The Miami Heat know a thing or two about dynamic duos.

Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo each scored 37 points in a 133-121 win over the Cleveland Cavaliers on Friday, Nov. 13. Antetokounmpo added nine rebounds and Adebayo notched 14 boards for a double-double in the NBA Cup matchup at the Kaseya Center.

According to the NBA, the two stars join LeBron James and Dwyane Wade as the only other duo in franchise history to score more than 35 points each in the same game.

James and Wade did so twice after James joined Wade on the Heat via "The Decision" in 2010. On March 14, 2012, Wade scored 36 points and James added 35 in a loss to the Chicago Bulls. They also reached the mark on Feb. 26, 2013 when James had 40 points and Wade tossed in 39 in a double-overtime win over the Sacramento Kings. The two won back-to-back championships in 2012 and 2013.

On Friday, Davion Mitchell added 22 points and 17 assists for Miami in the winning effort. Mitchell's 17 assists matched his career high.

Donovan Mitchell led Cleveland with 25 points, seven assists and four rebounds.

This is Antetokounmpo's first season in Miami after a blockbuster trade with the Milwaukee Bucks that included Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr. and Kasparas Jakučionis. The No. 15 overall pick in the 2013 NBA Draft spent his entire career up to this point with the Bucks and decided he wanted a fresh start. He won two league MVPs, was named an All-Star 10 times and won the 2021 NBA Finals in Milwaukee, when he was named Finals MVP.

He will face his former team for the first time on Nov. 18 when the Heat host "A Night in Vice City" to promote the highly-anticipated "Grand Theft Auto 6" video game.

Antetokounmpo is averaging 27.7 points, 12.6 rebounds and 5.2 assists per game this season. Adebayo, who is in his 10th NBA season, all with the Heat, is posting 17.8 points, 8.4 boards, 3.3 assists and a career-high 2.2 steals per outing so far this year. In March, he scored 83 points in a game, the second-most in NBA history.

#2715. UFC 334 predictions

UFC 334 is finally here to cap off one of the craziest weeks of MMA news this year.

We began with President Donald Trump supposedly asking his buddy Dana White to become the new White House press secretary—a hilarious joke, as it turns out—then former UFC heavyweight champion Andrei Arlovski seemingly made light of the death of past opponent Anthony Johnson—a simple misunderstanding, as it turns out—and THEN Usman Nurmagomedov led a gang beatdown on Merab Dvalishvili that led to all parties involved being temporarily detained and Nurmagomedov facing six months in prison.

Oh, and Tommy McMillen allegedly overdosed at a club in Arizona. But he's OK now!

After all that, Saturday night could end with Josh Hokit—yes, Josh freakin' Hokit—standing in the center of the octagon with the UFC undisputed heavyweight championship belt being wrapped around his waist, a little over a year after making his debut for the promotion.

Or, it could be Ciryl Gane cementing himself as heavyweight king, a title earned in the most winding way possible after poking Tom Aspinall in the eyes, winning an interim title by beating former two-division champion Alex Pereira, and then being promoted to undisputed status because Aspinall has been stuck on the sidelines. You know, because of the whole eye thing.

AND THEN we have the return of Amanda Nunes, one of the greatest fighters in MMA history, coming back from a three-year hiatus to finally settle her business with current bantamweight champion Kayla Harrison. It's one of the biggest matchups in women's MMA history, but could also signal the end of an era if both greats decide to hang it up under the Madison Square Garden lights. The whole thing is kind of surreal.

In other main card action, top 10 middleweight contender Caio Borralho defends his spot against dangerous kickboxer Yousri Belgaroui, welterweight knockout artist Uros Medic seeks another first-round finish when he faces Kevin Holland, and blue-chip flyweight prospect Bilal Hasan gets an opening showcase booking against Luis Gurule.

When: Saturday, Nov. 14. The four-fight early preliminary card begins at 5 p.m. ET, followed by a four-fight preliminary card at 7 p.m. ET. The five-fight main card begins at 9 p.m. ET with the entire event streaming live on Paramount+.

(Numbers in parentheses indicate standing in the MMA Fighting Global Rankings and Pound-for-Pound Rankings)

In theory, Ciryl Gane should have this. He's a far superior striker to Josh Hokit and has a combination of speed and agility that Hokit is yet to experience in his cagefighting career. Gane definitely has issues with consistency when it comes to big fights, but if he's on, he should cruise to victory.

The thing with Hokit is, he's defied all logic to even make it this far. So why should tonight be any different?

Shenanigans aside, there's a reason Hokit has been so successful and it's not just because of his razor-sharp wit. He's fearless, tough as hell, can definitely wrestle, and even if he's not as explosive as Gane, he's still in the elite tier of athletes at heavyweight. Tai Tuivasa once had Gane in danger just by coming forward and getting dumb with it. You think Hokit can't get dumb?

The fight completely changes if Hokit can find success with takedowns early. Hokit won't be afraid to eat punches to get in (even if he should be), and we know that Gane has been foiled by wrestling in the past. He might not be Jon Jones, but Hokit's wrestling is more than a notch above Francis Ngannou.

So why am I picking Gane? Remember what I just wrote about Hokit eating punches? That might fly with Curtis Blaydes, but prolonged striking exchanges with Gane rarely go well (Tom Aspinall had issues with Gane in the one round we saw them fight, Ngannou was losing the standup, and the aforementioned Tuivasa ended up getting knocked out). Even if Hokit's plan is to just wrestle, Gane's movement will give him headaches until he's left with no choice but to throw caution to the wind.

And that's when Gane connects and puts a pause on his championship dreams.

Look, this matchup is awesome, but we have our concerns.

Kayla Harrison, 36 years old with a lifetime of high-level combat sports under her belt, coming off of a major neck surgery.

Amanda Nunes, 38 years old with 28 pro fights to her name including numerous five-round championship bouts, coming off of a layoff of over 1,250 days.

This isn't Ronda Rousey vs. Gina Carano levels of concern, but suffice to say there's a reason both fighters in the co-main event have been the subject of retirement buzz. They've done it all in this business—except for fight each other.

On paper, it should be Nunes all day. As much as Harrison has evolved as a mixed martial artist over the past eight years, Nunes has a significant advantage in the striking department and I give her the jiu-jitsu edge, too. If Nunes wants to keep this on the feet and kickbox her way to victory, that's bad news for Harrison.

In Harrison's favor is the fact that she feels closer to her athletic prime than Nunes, and this is one of the rare times Nunes won't have a size and strength edge on her opponent. Harrison should have a lot of success in the clinch and on the ground when she gets Nunes down, and those grappling exchanges could sap Nunes' cardio ahead of the championship rounds.

That's where this fight gets decided. If you believe Nunes' time off has rejuvenated her and she's entering her comeback fight with a better comeback than ever, then the more skilled Nunes is the pick here; if you think Harrison being in fighting shape for the better part of a decade means she's more prepared, than you should pick Harrison to outlast Nunes.

I'm going with Harrison to take Nunes' best shots early and turn the tide in Round 3 before finishing an exhausted Nunes in the fourth.

This is the right matchup for Caio Borralho and Yousri Belgaroui, albeit a risky one.

Having fought many of his fellow contenders already, Borralho finds himself in a spot where it's either rematches or defending his number against up-and-coming names, and Belgaroui is the latter. Borralho got back in the win column with a solid performance against Reinier de Ridder in March, but still finds himself on the outside looking in as the 185-pound division waits for Sean Strickland to return.

The timing works perfectly for Belgaroui, an experienced kickboxer who can call himself both a past rival and current training partner of Alex Pereira. It's easy to see the "Poatan" comparisons as Belgaroui has a lethal mixture of technical skill, one-hit pop, and enough grappling defense to not be overwhelmed by the wrestlers and jiu-jitsu artists in the division.

That said, Belgaroui has had issues keeping the fight on his feet, with Mansur Abdul-Malik and Azamat Bekoev putting him on his back multiple times in his previous UFC appearances. However, neither of those opponents did much other than try to hold Belgaroui, and he went on to beat both of them. So the question is whether Borralho can muster up any meaningful offense on the ground or at least do a better job of winning standup exchanges when they materialize.

Borralho prides himself on mixing the martial arts, so for his sake let's hope he includes a healthy diet of single legs and body locks, and avoids the temptation of a kickboxing battle. I think he gets the job done.

Uros Medic has been making all the right moves at 170 pounds, scoring first-round knockout after first-round knockout, including a 30-second finish over Daniel Rodriguez in front of a roaring crowd in his native Serbia this past August. A top 10 opponent should have been next.

Unfortunately for Medic and the rest of the division, the cluster at the top needs to sort itself out first and at the moment, Medic isn't part of that equation. Rather than sit and wait for upcoming matchups to resolve, Medic instead accepted this fight with the unpredictable Kevin Holland. Given Holland's laissez-faire attitude to fight bookings, this looks like a good opportunity for Medic to beat a veteran with a substantial following.

My hesitation to go chalk here stems from the fact that Holland has had plenty of success with strikers in his day. Medic is a get-or-get-got guy and lately he's been doing the getting, but it feels like only a matter of time until he gets got again. That could be Saturday, especially if he's reckless against Holland, who has a pretty good chin and lively offense when he finds a rhythm.

It will be another first-round finish alright, but I actually like Holland to pull off the upset.

I'm all in on the Bilal Hasan hype, like, I get it, but this young man being 10-to-1 favorite in just his second UFC fight is crazy.

Hasan oozes star power, both with his effervescent personality and fun striking style, which involves plenty of trickery to set up his heavier offense. He'll have plenty of opportunity to style on Luis Gurule, who has been more than a step slow in losing four of his five UFC fights. This is Hasan's match to lose.

I just don't think any fighter with this little octagon experience that isn't an established name in another promotion or discipline should be given that much respect. Even with this being an obvious squash match, 10-to-1 odds for Hasan? Gurule should take this personally.

Don't get me wrong, I'm obviously picking Hasan (KO, Round 2), I just wanted to rant about odds for a sec and also explain why Gurule finding a way to eke out an upset wouldn't surprise me in the slightest. It's The Year of the (not Raw) Dog!

#2713. Saints sent Jordyn Tyson to renowned hamstring specialist at University of Wisconsin

In 2021, the NFL awarded a $4 million grant to Dr. Bryan Heiderscheit and his team at the University of Wisconsin to research new ways to prevent and treat hamstring injuries. Saints rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson may benefit from that research.

Mike Triplett of NewOrleans.Football reports that the Saints sent Tyson on two separate visits to the University of Wisconsin to be evaluated by Dr. Heiderscheit and his team.

Hamstring injuries have been a major problem for Tyson, who was out for three months with a hamstring injury before finally making his NFL debut last week. Tyson also missed time at Arizona State last year because of a hamstring injury, and he didn't run at either Arizona State's Pro Day or the NFL Scouting Combine because of his hamstring.

But there's hope for Tyson after his evaluations in Wisconsin. Heiderscheit was able to identify a weakness with Tyson's hamstring that he thinks can be strengthened with a specific workout regimen that Tyson has been following.

Heiderscheit previously worked with Packers wide receiver Christian Watson and helped him recover from hamstring injuries, and it worked: Watson has started every game this season and in nine games already has career-highs with 49 catches for 879 yards, and he's leading the NFL with an average of 17.9 yards per catch.

That's the kind of player the Saints think Tyson can be, if he can stay healthy. Heiderscheit's treatment may be the key to Tyson staying healthy.

#2712. Utah Jazz vs. Houston Rockets: Recap and Final Score

Nov 13, 2026; Houston, Texas, USA; Utah Jazz guard Darryn Peterson (22) handles the ball against Houston Rockets center Alperen Sengun (28) during the first quarter at Toyota Center. Mandatory Credit: Erik Williams-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The Utah Jazz fall to the Houston Rockets 125-118 for their twelfth loss of the season, and second NBA Cup game loss.

The Jazz got off to a solid start in the first quarter with respectable defense and ball movement. Although no one could stop Alpren Sengun, who was getting everything he wanted all night long (including every foul call), Jaxon Hayes and Mo Bamba punished his poor drop coverage on the other end by catching lobs.

After the first quarter, the game was tied up at 27 a piece. Jaxon Hayes came out of the game with an injury (the Jazz can't catch a break with the frontcourt injuries!). Like every other game this season, the bench came in and immediately started turning the ball over and giving up easy baskets, putting the Jazz in a 10-point deficit going into the second half.

Then it got exciting. Darryn Peterson and Keyonte George took over the game, attacking the rim, spraying out the 3-point shooters, and getting stops on the other end. Ace Bailey was hitting his 3s, Keyonte had an amazing 4-point play, and Darryn was controling the game and getting any shot he wanted. Before long, the 10-point deficit became a 10-point lead. Utah's offense was looking as good as it had all season. Darryn Peterson scored 12 points in the first 6 minutes of the third quarter.

But apparently Will Hardy wanted to change things. Enter: Isaiah Collier and Brice Sensabaugh. Instead of going with what was clearly working, Isaiah Collier pounded the air out of the ball as the lead was erased almost as quickly as it was built.

It was about to get ugly again, but Keyonte George came alive, scoring 23 points in the second half. He was aggressive, attacking the basket and creating contact, but the refs decided only the Rockets were allowed to shoot free throws this game.

Bamba wasn't doing anything to stop Sengun, who scored pretty much every time he touched the basketball within 15 feet of the rim. Tony Bradley also played 12 minutes, but didn't do much to stop him either.

However, despite the bench, the refs, and Sengun, the Jazz were still in it. After a beautiful jumper at the elbow from Peterson, the Jazz were down one with 2:40 to go. Amen Thompson scored to put Houston up three, and Keyonte had a terrible turnover, trying to dump the ball down to Bamba. After George's turnover, Sensabaugh bricked an offbalance lay, and Sengun scored on the other end.

With 11 seconds left in the game, the Jazz were down 5. Any reasonable person would have assumed a play would be drawn up for Darryn to score. But no. Not only did that not happen, but he was benched for none of than Svi Mykhailiuk.

Sensabaugh got the ball and did nothing other than jump out of bounds and try to get a foul call.

Another heartbreaking loss in a very winnable game. The bench is horrendous and Will Hardy continues to make mind boggling decisions with the game on the line. Why did we tank all year for Peterson if we are just going to play Brice and Svi at the end of games!?!?

The young core of the Jazz played great, but it wasn't enough. Keyonte, Ace, and Darryn have very bright futures.

Alpren Sengun had 43 points and 12 rebounds.

Kevin Durant did what he does, scoring 22 points without hardly breaking a sweat.

Darryn Peterson finished with 28 points and 7 rebounds for his fifth straight 20-point game. This season has been rough, but at least we have Darryn Peterson.

#2711. Scaling the Rocks: Carrigg and Karros turn two at Wrigley

Here's what's going on with the Colorado Rockies and the rest of Major League Baseball.

There were some outstanding defensive plays made by the Colorado Rockies in 2026, but Purple Row readers have spoken. Cole Carrigg and Kyle Karros' remarkable 8-5 double play against the Chicago Cubs on June 17 has been voted the Rockies' Defensive Play of the Year.

The Rockies were trailing 8-2 in the bottom of the fifth inning at Wrigley Field when Matt Shaw lifted a 345-foot fly ball into straightaway center field. Carrigg tracked it down, getting behind the baseball and positioning himself to make a throw to third base, where Ian Happ was attempting to advance.

Carrigg made the catch and unleashed a 99.8-mph throw toward third, generating so much momentum that he went tumbling into a barrel roll after releasing the baseball.

The ball arrived on the infield side of third base, forcing Karros to reach out to make the catch before lunging back toward the bag. He managed to apply the tag to Happ just before the runner reached third, completing the double play.

It was an outstanding throw by Carrigg and an equally impressive piece of glove work by Karros. And considering the two are best friends, it's fitting that they combined for one of the most memorable defensive moments of the season.

Carrigg's arm strength was hardly a secret by the end of 2026. He averaged 96.9 mph on his qualifying outfield throws, ranking fourth among MLB outfielders and second among center fielders, behind only Oneil Cruz. His throw against the Cubs was among the hardest of the season to record an out.

The play didn't ultimately change the outcome of the game. Colorado chipped away at Chicago's lead but eventually fell 8-6.

Perhaps the best reaction came from the Cubs broadcast, where the announcer couldn't help but admire what he'd just witnessed.

How Colorado's depth could help DePodesta make moves this offseason | MLB.com

Thomas Harding spoke with Rockies president of baseball operations Paul DePodesta about the team's positional depth and how it might factor into offseason moves. DePodesta believes Colorado has seven or eight MLB-ready outfielders and acknowledged that there simply isn't room for everyone. He also confirmed that the team's surplus has already come up in trade discussions. We've spent plenty of time talking about the possibility of moving position players to acquire pitching, and it sounds like the front office is exploring those options as well. The Rockies have some interesting young talent, but figuring out how to turn that depth into pitching could be one of DePodesta's most important tasks this offseason.

Could trading Hunter Goodman be in play for Rockies? | Denver Sports (Podcast)

Speaking of potential trades, the Shapiro and Piro podcast from Denver Sports discusses whether the Rockies should consider moving All-Star catcher Hunter Goodman. It's an interesting question. Goodman is one of Colorado's most productive players and could certainly be part of the team's future. On the other hand, he's also one of the few players on the roster who might bring back a substantial pitching return. Trading him would be a difficult decision, but it's one the Rockies should at least be willing to consider.

Rockies' Rising Offense May Be Just Getting Started | Sports Illustrated

Maddy Dickens of Sports Illustrated is optimistic about Colorado's offense heading into 2027. With young players like Cole Carrigg and Charlie Condon entering the picture, Dickens believes the Rockies could reach 80 wins next season if they can add some average pitching. That's quite a leap for a team coming off 104 losses, but hey, we could all use a little hopium this offseason.

Baseball's Payroll Disparity Problem Explained. The Case for a Salary Cap and Floor | MLB.com

MLB executive vice president of baseball operations Morgan Sword lays out the league's argument for a salary cap, salary floor, and expanded revenue sharing ahead of the next round of collective bargaining. The video focuses on the growing payroll disparity between clubs and how MLB believes its proposed changes could improve competitive balance. Of course, the MLBPA sees things differently and has strongly opposed a salary cap. With the possibility of a work stoppage hanging over the next CBA negotiations, it's worth hearing the league's position directly, even if you don't agree with its proposed solution.

New Top 100 MLB Prospect Rankings for 2026-27 Offseason | Bleacher Report

Joel Reuter released his updated Top 100 prospect rankings, and four Rockies made the list. Ethan Holliday checks in at No. 35, followed by Charlie Condon (47), Roldy Brito (55), and Tyler Bell (91). It's nice to see Colorado represented, but there's a familiar theme here: all four are position players. The Rockies have assembled some intriguing young offensive talent, but developing pitching remains a significant organizational challenge.

Wheeler, Alvarez earn MLB Comeback Player of the Year awards | Associated Press

Awards season continues with Zack Wheeler and Yordan Alvarez taking home the National League and American League Comeback Player of the Year awards. The Associated Press also provides a rundown of several other honors, including the Hank Aaron Awards for Alvarez and Pete Crow-Armstrong, Relievers of the Year Mason Miller and Bryan Baker, and Executive of the Year Erik Neander. There's plenty to discuss as baseball continues handing out its 2026 hardware.

2027 Contemporary Baseball Era Committee Candidate: Dusty Baker | FanGraphs

Jay Jaffe of FanGraphs takes a deep dive into Dusty Baker's remarkable life and career as the longtime manager gets another opportunity at the Hall of Fame. Baker's story goes well beyond the dugout. He fished with Satchel Paige, spent time with Jimi Hendrix, managed five franchises to the postseason, and eventually won a World Series. Jaffe examines the successes, controversies, and disappointments along the way while making the case for Baker's induction. If you enjoy baseball history, this is a terrific read.

#2710. Fabiani svela la scelta di Gattuso: “Prima opzione, non abbiamo avuto dubbi”

Il ds racconta la scelta di Gattuso: prima opzione di Lazio e Lotito. Poi l’elogio al tecnico della capolista.

Lazio, Fabiani esalta Gattuso: “Sta dirigendo alla grande l’orchestra”

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Gennaro Gattuso era la prima scelta della Lazio. Nessun ripiego e, soprattutto, nessun dubbio da parte del direttore sportivo Angelo Fabiani e del presidente Claudio Lotito. A raccontare i retroscena della scelta dell’allenatore è stato lo stesso dirigente biancoceleste.

Fabiani, parlando della Lazio capolista di Serie A, ha riservato parole importanti a Gattuso. Il ds ne ha sottolineato soprattutto la capacità di rapportarsi con calciatori e dirigenti, utilizzando poi una metafora significativa: “Gli abbiamo dato la bacchetta e lui sta dirigendo alla grande l’orchestra”.

Secondo quanto riportato da La Gazzetta dello Sport, Fabiani ha spiegato innanzitutto quanto sia importante scegliere un tecnico nel momento più adatto: “Gli allenatori sono tutti giusti, ma vanno anche presi al momento giusto”.

L’esperienza maturata nei diversi club della sua carriera ha portato Fabiani a una convinzione precisa sul ruolo dell’allenatore.

“Ne ho avuti tanti nei vari club in cui ho lavorato. Chi non è andato bene è solo perché era arrivato nel momento sbagliato”.

Una situazione che, secondo il direttore sportivo, non riguarda certamente Gattuso. La Lazio aveva infatti individuato subito in Rino il profilo sul quale puntare.

“È stata la nostra prima opzione. Lotito è un presidente che lascia ampia libertà sul mercato, sulla scelta dell’allenatore però è presente”.

Fabiani ha quindi chiarito come la decisione sia stata condivisa con il presidente biancoceleste: “Ma io e lui non abbiamo avuto dubbi nel puntare su Rino. Le sue grandi qualità le conoscevamo bene”.

Il dirigente della Lazio è entrato poi nel dettaglio delle caratteristiche che maggiormente apprezza dell’allenatore.

“Gattuso è stato un campione formidabile, che ha vinto tutto”.

Il valore aggiunto, però, secondo Fabiani va ricercato soprattutto nel modo in cui il tecnico riesce a gestire i rapporti all’interno del club.

“Ma la sua grandezza è mettere tutto questo da parte nel rapporto con i giocatori e con i dirigenti”.

Da qui la frase con cui il direttore sportivo sintetizza il lavoro svolto finora dal tecnico alla guida della Lazio:

“Noi gli abbiamo dato la bacchetta e lui sta dirigendo alla grande l’orchestra”.

#2707. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2706. Orioles news: Notable free agents are starting to sign

Despite the unknowns of the next CBA, teams are starting to get a little busy this offseason. Emilio Pagán agreed to a deal with the Tigers on Tuesday, Evan Phillips inked a three-year contract with the Braves on Thursday, and then just yesterday World Series champ Jake Bauers joined the Red Sox on a four-year pact.

Bauers was one of the best hitters available in what is an admittedly thin free agent class. He had an outstanding 2026 season, slashing .266/.389/.484 with 26 home runs as a 30-year-old. The campaign sticks out like a sore thumb in an MLB career. According to Baseball Reference, Bauers was worth 3.3 bWAR in 2026 alone, bringing his career bWAR up from the red to 2.0. The Red Sox will be betting that he is simply a late bloomer and can largely maintain that performance moving forward.

FanGraphs had projected Bauers, who did have a qualifying offer attached to him, would get a three-year deal worth $51 million ($17 million AAV). Instead, he gets four years at $58 million ($14.5 million) from Boston. Phillips had a projection of one year at $6.8 million. He was able to land a three-year deal worth $35 million ($11.67 AAV) in Atlanta.

The Bauers deal feels fair. He got less AAV but an additional year despite the QO. That's pretty good. Phillips, a former Oriole that was born in Salisbury, has to be ecstatic about his new contract. He barely pitched between the end of 2024 and this past July due to injuries to his rotator cuff and then Tommy John surgery. But he was great towards the end of this past season and likely factors into high-leverage innings for Atlanta.

What does all of that mean? Honestly, who knows. Public projections often differ from how team's are evaluating talent internally. But it certainly doesn't seem like teams are too worried about the talk of a salary cap, at least not for 2027 anyway. MLB Trade Rumors explains that the Red Sox exceeded the 2026 CBT threshold and are on pace to do so again in 2027, if the system is in place. The signing of Phillips will push the Braves close to the line as well.

All that to say that if the Orioles were hoping Trevor Rogers might give them a discount on account of everyone being artificially strapped for cash, they had better think again. There is money to be spent, and it could come sooner than later, regardless of what's happening behind the scenes.

Mariners Notes: Infield Needs, Trade Candidates, Sloan | MLB Trade RumorsGunnar Henderson and Jordan Westburg are listed as potential trade candidates that fit what the Mariners are looking for. The O's and M's have long seemed like good partners due to the former's glut of infielders and the latter's wealth of pitchers. And yet, nothing has happened. Maybe that changes this winter.

This, that and the other | Roch KubatkoRoch touches on the Orioles closing situation. Ryan Helsley and Félix Bautista are both likely to factor in, but injuries are a concern. Yennier Cano has closing experience, though he has never really been a fit in the ninth inning. The team needs a real backup plan. How much they are willing to pay for it is unclear.

As a lockout looms, MLB teams say it's 'business as usual.' Is it really? | The Baltimore BannerObviously not. But what else are they gonna say? MLB will have their next season at some point, and the holes on a team's roster are not going to fix themselves, so they have to make moves to address them. It won't all happen overnight, and it's quite likely that there will be a multi-week/month pause in the middle. But for now, they do what they can.

Freddy Galvis turns 37 today. He spent part of the 2021 seasona s the Orioles everyday shortstop before being dealt to the Phillies for a minor leaguer.

Curt Schilling is 60 years old. His storied 20-season MLB career began in Baltimore, where he spent parts of three seasons from 1988 through '90. The Orioles' decision to then trade him, along with Steve Finley and Pete Harnisch, to the Astros in exchange for Glenn Davis is widely regarded as the worst trade in team history.

1973 – Jim Palmer is named AL Cy Young after winning 22 games and leading the league with a 2.40 ERA. The 28-year-old Palmer is a first-time winner and will go on to earn the award twice more in his Hall of Fame career.

2005 – The Orioles announce that neither Sammy Sosa nor Rafael Palmeiro will be returning to the team next season. Both players claim they wish to keep playing. Sosa will eventually sign back with the Rangers, but not until 2007. Palmeiro never gets another MLB deal.

#2703. Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return

Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

PG-13 was rated R in his return to Philadelphia.

The middle finger Paul George directed toward one baseline fan only reinforced that rating.

Tuesday night was expected to revolve around Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum sharing an NBA court as opponents for the first time. Instead, the other headliner in the summer's blockbuster trade stole the show.

George scored a game-high 36 points in Boston's 123-101 win over the Sixers. He shot 14 for 22 from the floor, made six of his 11 three-point attempts and scored 14 consecutive Boston points in the fourth quarter.

The game was tied at 79 with 3:19 remaining in the third quarter. Boston outscored Philadelphia 44-22 from that point forward.

The Celtics went nine minutes and 20 seconds without making a two-point field goal during the second half. Instead, they made nine consecutive field goals from three, the second-longest such streak by a Sixers opponent over the last 30 seasons.

Payton Pritchard opened the fourth with consecutive threes. George followed with eight straight points, helping the Celtics begin the quarter on a 14-0 run that turned a competitive game into a rout.

George's return carried a complicated history. His two seasons with the Sixers were repeatedly interrupted by injuries, but he also played a significant role in their most memorable playoff run in years.

Last spring, George helped the Sixers overcome a 3-1 deficit to eliminate Boston in seven games. He averaged 17.4 points and shot 55 percent from three during the series.

Tyrese Maxey was happy to see his former teammate Tuesday, even if he disliked what followed.

"It was good to see Paul," Maxey said. "I love him, love his family. … He gave us everything he had while he was here. We know what he did in the playoffs last year. Great person, great family, and we'll see him again."

Maxey then added one important qualifier.

George instead scored from nearly everywhere.

"He had some open threes. He had some pull-up threes. He had some middies," Maxey said. "He played within the game, too. That's what Paul does. He plays within the game. He takes what the defense gives him, and we gave him too many open looks tonight.

"PG, we know what PG does. We shouldn't even be allowing him to get up 11 threes, and that's on us."

Nick Nurse watched George attack the Sixers in several ways.

"He really had it going," Nurse said. "He'd post up, and-one, fallaways. He went down the lane, high archer off the glass, and-one. He scored in about every way he could tonight."

George heard boos during his return and said the arena carried the atmosphere, though not quite the intensity, of a playoff game.

"This building can be very electric as well," George said. "It was fun. It was fun to play in this environment."

One interaction extended beyond the usual reception for a returning player.

During a stoppage, the ball rolled toward a fan seated along the baseline. George said the fan looked directly at him before dropping the ball instead of returning it.

"There was a fan being an a–," George said. "The ball rolled to him. He looked me dead in my eyes, dropped the ball on the ground as if I'm a dog to go fetch or go get it, instead of passing the ball to me like a normal fan would do.

"And so, yeah, then I rolled him a middle finger in return."

#2700. Nationwide ground stop potentially complicates NFL, college games

The sudden nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA will potentially impact this weekend’s football games.

It’s only the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11. It’s apparently due to a widespread outage impacting air-traffic control functions.

Visiting NFL teams typically travel to the sites of their games on Saturday; if the situation lingers, some teams may not be able to get to where they need to be. More immediately, college teams that travel on Friday have a mess.

As noted by Matt Maiocco of NBC Sports Bay Area, the 49ers usually travel on Friday for games that are at least two time zones away. For Sunday’s game against the Cowboys, they plan to travel on Saturday.

Some teams can get to the locations of their games by car or train. The distance from Minneapolis to Green Bay is 279 miles. For Buffalo to New Jersey (for Bills-Jets), it’s also less than 300 miles.

It’s roughly 290 miles fom Pittsburgh to Cincinnati, and 373 miles from L.A. to Phoenix.

For the other games (particularly Chargers-Ravens on Monday night), it’s a long way to go via ground transportation.

#2699. John Harbaugh: Cam Skattebo was not supposed to push on Jameis Winston sneak

Giants coach John Harbaugh defended running back Cam Skattebo, who stayed in his stance on a crucial Jameis Winston quarterback sneak during Thursday night’s loss to the Commanders.

Harbaugh said the call was a quarterback sneak but not a tush push, and Skattebo wasn’t supposed to be pushing Winston.

“We had a certain check involved in it, so he wasn’t supposed to be up there pushing. We didn’t call the same [QB sneak] that we’ve been calling,” Harbaugh said, via Pat Leonard of the New York Daily News. “What else am I supposed to say? He wasn’t supposed to be up there pushing.”

Why the Giants wouldn’t want Skattebo to push Winston in an attempt to get the first down yardage is unclear, but the play looked strange, and it was a big one for the Giants, who had a 21-17 lead late in the fourth quarter at the time, but couldn’t hold the lead after getting stuffed on that quarterback sneak and lost 24-21.
