#2698. Four things to watch as Sixers look to respond against Raptors

Four things to watch as Sixers look to respond against Raptors originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers will not need to wait long for an opportunity to move past their most lopsided loss of the season.

Less than 48 hours after Boston's 123-101 win exposed several of Philadelphia's early weaknesses, the Sixers will host the Toronto Raptors on Thursday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

The Raptors are coming off a difficult meeting with the Celtics, too. Toronto led Boston by 22 points Wednesday before being outscored 61-34 over the final 29:24 of a 98-93 loss.

Philadelphia enters at 9-3 following Tuesday's defeat. Toronto is 5-6 and will complete a back-to-back and its third game in four nights.

LeBron James has been ruled out because of low-back and sciatica management. Joel Embiid is questionable with right plantar fascia injury management. Toronto will be without Kawhi Leonard, Scottie Barnes and Nate Bittle.

Here are four areas to watch as the Sixers try to respond.

Few teams have forced opponents into mistakes as frequently as Toronto.

The Raptors have generated 18.9 turnovers per game, the highest mark in the NBA. They are also averaging 10.9 steals and nearly 15 offensive rebounds.

The Sixers have countered that type of pressure well. Their 13.0 turnovers per game are tied for one of the lowest marks in the league.

Toronto's length remains disruptive even without Leonard and Barnes. The Raptors regularly crowd ball handlers, reach into passing lanes and send multiple players toward the offensive glass. Jakob Poeltl supplies size inside while RJ Barrett, Ja'Kobe Walter and Collin Murray-Boyles can create problems away from the ball.

The Raptors' pressure can punish a careless pass twice. It takes away a Sixers possession and gives Toronto an opportunity to score before the defense gets organized.

Philadelphia has largely avoided those mistakes while adjusting to a new lineup and playing at a quicker pace. Maintaining that control without James, who has handled a significant share of the playmaking, will be one of Thursday's clearest challenges.

Toronto has not built its offense around half-court shooting.

The Raptors are averaging 49.6 paint points and 16.4 fast-break points. Even while shorthanded Wednesday, they scored 18 points in transition against Boston.

That presents a direct test for a Sixers defense allowing 16.5 fast-break points per game, the fourth-highest figure in the NBA. Philadelphia has also surrendered 49.5 paint points per contest.

The first concern will be slowing the ball.

Immanuel Quickley returned Wednesday after missing two games with right hamstring soreness. He gives Toronto another guard capable of attacking early in the shot clock, while Barrett has consistently looked to get downhill with Leonard and Barnes unavailable.

Poeltl can create scoring chances without having a play called for him. He runs the floor, screens for Toronto's guards, rolls toward the rim and cleans up misses.

The Sixers have been effective in transition themselves, averaging 17.1 fast-break points. Maxey and VJ Edgecombe can change ends quickly after a stop, but Philadelphia must secure the ball first.

Thursday's game could swing on which team gets to run and which one is forced to create against a set defense.

Toronto provided an extreme example Wednesday of how quickly the three-point line can alter a game.

The Raptors entered their matchup against Boston shooting 31.8 percent from beyond the arc. They proceeded to hit 10 of their 18 attempts in the first quarter, tying a franchise record for threes in a period.

They went 6 for 25 over the final three quarters.

After Wednesday, Toronto is shooting 32.4 percent from three this season. The Sixers should not treat the Raptors like an elite perimeter team. They also cannot allow them to find early confidence through uncovered catch-and-shoot attempts.

Walter made five threes Wednesday and scored a team-high 17 points. Rookie Allen Graves added 13 points, while Quickley, Barrett and Jamison Battle are all willing shooters when the ball reaches them in rhythm.

Philadelphia's problems against Boston extended beyond the Celtics making difficult shots. The Sixers were late on several closeouts and occasionally allowed too much separation while navigating screens.

Toronto does not rely on the three as heavily as Boston. Wednesday showed it can still build a lead quickly when those shots start falling.

The Raptors expended significant energy Wednesday before traveling to Philadelphia.

They scored 38 first-quarter points, built a 22-point lead and then watched Boston erase the entire margin before the end of the third quarter. Quickley and Barrett each played more than 31 minutes. Poeltl and Walter both played at least 29.

The Sixers should have the fresher legs. Whether they take advantage could become apparent early.

Philadelphia has averaged 26.3 first-quarter points with a minus-2.2 scoring margin in opening periods. Slow starts have forced the Sixers to play from behind several times, including in their 29-point comeback against Cleveland.

An aggressive start would make Toronto respond quickly after a draining loss. Maxey and Edgecombe can apply pressure by pushing the ball after defensive rebounds instead of allowing the Raptors to set their pressure defense.

James' absence will require an adjustment. Maxey, Brown and Anfernee Simons should handle more of the ball and more of the decisions that come with initiating the offense.

If Embiid plays, the Sixers can make Toronto work through Poeltl by establishing him inside. If Embiid sits, Philadelphia's size concerns will become more pronounced with Adem Bona, Dominick Barlow and Ariel Hukporti also unavailable.

The Sixers have a rest advantage against a depleted opponent coming off an emotional loss. Their response should begin well before the fourth quarter.

#2694. Observations after Sixers lose 1st Brown vs. Tatum matchup, George scores 36

Observations after Sixers lose 1st Brown vs. Tatum matchup, George scores 36 originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Round 1 of the new-look Sixers vs. the new-look Celtics decisively went Boston's way on Tuesday night.

In the first meeting between the teams since the July trade that sent Jaylen Brown to Philadelphia and Paul George to Boston, the Celtics earned a 123-101 win at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

The Sixers dropped to 9-3 and the Celtics improved to 9-2.

George was the game's brightest star, scoring 36 points on 14-for-22 shooting. Jayson Tatum added 21 points.

Tyrese Maxey's 24 points led the Sixers. Brown was hampered by foul trouble in his heavily anticipated first outing against Tatum. He posted 13 points, five rebounds and two assists in 26 minutes.

The Sixers will host the Raptors on Thursday night. Here are observations on their blowout loss to the Celtics:

To no one's surprise, Brown and Tatum guarded each other to open the night.

VJ Edgecombe defended a former teammate in George, who scored Boston's first four points with a pair of pure jumpers. On the other end, Maxey made the Sixers' first three field goals.

Judging by volume, the home fans cared most about the much-scrutinized Brown vs. Tatum matchup. The crowd was excited early when Brown snagged a steal and then dished to Maxey for a fast-break three-pointer. The fans also dialed up the noise when Brown sized up Tatum in isolation. He wound up dribbling the ball off his foot and out of bounds. Tatum pointed to signal it was Celtics ball.

Boston's star forward had a productive first quarter, posting 11 points. He scored an easy two when he used a back screen to break free from Brown and convert a layup that put the Celtics up 11-7. Boston began 9 for 12 from the floor as a team.

As for Brown, he sat shortly after being called for his second foul with 6:48 left in the first quarter.

Brown re-entered at the start of the second quarter. The Sixers still struggled to eat into Boston's lead.

A Sam Hauser triple extended the Celtics' advantage to 12 points. There was some audible frustration in the building after Brown missed two free throws on the next possesion.

The Sixers' deficit hit 16 points on a Hugo Gonzalez jumper. Meanwhile, the Sixers missed 12 of their first 14 three-point tries. While some of those shots were open looks that simply didn't go down, the Sixers also rushed up several contested jumpers before they made Boston's defense do serious work.

In the bigger picture, it wouldn't be remotely surprising if shooting stands out as a weak area for the Sixers come the trade deadline. They entered the game ranked 27th in the NBA in three-point frequency outside of garbage time and 22nd in three-point accuracy, according to Cleaning the Glass.

Joel Embiid (16 points, six rebounds) had an injury scare late in the second quarter when he fell hard after missing a layup in transition. He rose gingerly and limped through the final 30 seconds or so of the first half.

The Sixers' star big man was fine to start the third quarter and even drained a long-overdue three on the opening possession. He'd been in a terrible outside shooting slump (3 for 32 from deep on the season) before that shot.

Brown's foul trouble persisted. He picked up his fourth personal with 10:40 to go in the third quarter.

The Sixers stormed back without him and their defense played a large role. After LeBron James rumbled in for a layup, Dean Wade stonewalled Payton Pritchard on the perimeter to force a shot-clock violation. Wade later canned a three to even the contest at 76-all.

The Celtics responded and Tatum led the charge. His third-quarter exploits included a highlight slam on James and a top-of-the-key three to build Boston's lead back up to nine points.

Pritchard buried a three on the first possession of the fourth quarter and the Celtics' advantage kept growing. George celebrated a triple that stretched his team's lead to 100-82. The Sixers' spirits were considerably lower as they headed to their bench for a timeout. As a Sixer, George only had one higher-scoring game (39 points) than his performance Tuesday.

George and Tatum were each excellent in Philadelphia. Outside of Maxey, who finished 8 for 12 from the field, the Sixers didn't receive similar games from their stars.

Brown will be back in Boston on Jan. 21 when the Sixers visit the Celtics. He'll try to even the score.

#2689. Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win

Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers brushed off their blowout loss to the Celtics and got back in the win column Thursday night.

They overcame a first-quarter deficit as high as 17 points and earned a 123-112 home win over the Raptors. The Sixers moved to 10-3 and Toronto fell to 5-7.

Tyrese Maxey had 27 points and eight assists. Joel Embiid added 20 points.

Jaylen Brown tallied 18 points and six rebounds. VJ Edgecombe posted 15 points, eight rebounds and a season-high eight assists. Anfernee Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range.

RJ Barrett recorded 31 points and 14 rebounds. Immanuel Quickley had 26 points and six assists.

The Sixers were without LeBron James (low back/sciatica management), Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain), Dominick Barlow (lower back stress reaction) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear).

The team told reporters Thursday morning that Bona will be re-evaluated in approximately one week and that Barlow participated in shootaround. The 23-year-old forward also went through a pregame workout on the Xfinity Mobile Arena floor. There's no formal timetable for his return.

Toronto's sidelined players included Kawhi Leonard and Scottie Barnes.

The Sixers will face the Pacers on Sunday afternoon in Philadelphia. Here are observations on their victory over the Raptors:

Dean Wade began the game in James' normal spot. The Sixers started slowly, missing their first foul field goals and opening 1 for 8 from three-point range.

He stayed down after setting a ball screen and having an apparent knee-to-knee collision with Ja'Kobe Walter. The Sixers called timeout with 8:30 left in the first quarter and Embiid grabbed at his right knee. He eventually rose with assistance from teammates and Sixers head athletic trainer Kevin Johnson, then limped back to the locker room. Jabari Walker entered.

At the 5:26 mark of the first quarter, Embiid checked back in to cheers from the home fans.

"I knew that he didn't twist it or anything," Maxey said. "I knew it was a knee-to-knee, so I wasn't too worried. He kept saying, 'I just got kneed.' That still hurts, though."

Embiid ended up logging 28 minutes, though he certainly wanted to play more.

"He was very, very motivated to play," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "It was hard to get him out for his scheduled rests tonight, which is a good problem sometimes."

While Embiid's return was a major positive development, the Sixers fell further behind. The Raptors' lead swelled to 32-16 with a Jamison Battle three-pointer and Nurse burned a timeout.

Simons sunk a buzzer-beating three to conclude the first quarter, cutting the Sixers' deficit to nine points.

"Those are big momentum plays that usually have some weight to them and carry you into the next moment," Nurse said.

The Sixers kept rolling against a shorthanded Toronto team playing on the second night of a back-to-back. Simons nailed a triple to kick off the scoring in the second quarter. Brown buried a mid-range jumper and Edgecombe jammed in a crowd-pleasing dunk to give the Sixers a 35-34 edge.

Brown and Edgecombe shined in the second quarter both as individuals and as a duo. The Sixers need Edgecombe to attack a bit more offensively when he shares the floor with Brown and bench players. It doesn't hurt for the second-year guard to have that clarity about his role in those units.

"He's one of our better playmakers," Maxey said of Edgecombe. "He's really good at getting downhill and creating for himself and others."

The Sixers' only three bench rotation players were Walker, Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope (11 points, five assists). In addition to Walker, Wade got center minutes behind Embiid.

Embiid picked up his third foul with 2:23 left in the second quarter and had to take a seat. The teams were tied at 60 apiece through two periods.

The game remained even for much of the third, but Maxey fueled an 11-0 Sixers run late in the quarter.

His speed and the Sixers' collective focus on pushing the pace whenever possible allowed the team to get regular points before Toronto could set its defense. Maxey zoomed in for a layup, then tossed the ball ahead to Brown for an easy bucket. Brown assisted a Simons three. Walker converted a fast-break lay-in and canned a three on the first possession of the fourth quarter. All of a sudden, the Sixers held a 101-87 lead.

Brown, Edgecombe and the bench gave the Sixers more good minutes early in the fourth quarter. They sealed the deal without any late drama. And the fans chanting for a Tacko Fall appearance got their wish with a final-minute entrance by the 7-foot-6 center.

#2688. After his father's death, 49ers' Corliss Waitman found purpose amid his pain

Corliss Waitman was born in Belgium, grew up in the Netherlands and owns the obscure distinction of being the only left-footed Black player at his position in NFL history.

There is, quite literally, no one quite like the San Francisco 49ers punter, but so many can relate to what drove him to the highest level of professional success: He wanted to honor his father.

In 2013, Waitman, a senior at Milton (Fla.) High School, was being recruited by Oregon and Auburn, two years after the Ducks and Tigers played in the national championship game. But he passed on the bluebloods. His heart was set on a startup: the University of South Alabama, which began playing football in 2009.

Waitman's dad, Jose, played basketball at South Alabama before embarking on a 15-season professional career in Europe. In 1987, he was named MVP of a Dutch league.

Jose Waitman, 6-foot-9 and 220 pounds during his playing days, was a towering presence in Corliss' life. He died at 48 on April 17, 2013, when Corliss was 17. Months later, Corliss sent an email to a coach at a fledgling program a year removed from a 2-11 season that didn't know he was interested. He asked if the staff could recruit him.

"I went to South Alabama," Corliss said, "solely to honor my dad."

During a stellar debut season with the 49ers, Waitman, 31, recently reflected on his improbable journey and the role his father played in it. After signing a one-year deal in March, Waitman ranks fifth in the NFL in net punting average (44.0 yards) and has dropped 47.6% of his kicks inside the 20-yard line, ranking 10th. He was named the NFC Special Teams Player of the Week after pinning all five of his punts inside the 20, including three inside the 10, in the 49ers' 32-29 win at Seattle on Oct. 11.

Niners punter Corliss Waitman was named the NFC Special Teams Player of the Week after pinning all five of his punts inside the 20 in a 32-29 win in Seattle on Oct. 11. (Alika Jenner/Getty Images)

The honor was another step in Waitman's nomadic NFL career, a journey he didn't see coming. He grew up playing soccer in Europe and was blessed with a bazooka left leg. But when he was introduced to football shortly after arriving in the United States at 14, he was comically inconsistent. He didn't become Milton's full-time punter until his senior season.

Waitman quickly ascended to all-state, a transformation that began in the months after his father died from the complications of a stroke. Chafan Marsh, Waitman's high school coach who was close friends with Jose, said Jose's death gave Corliss purpose as he dealt with his pain.

In the months that followed, Corliss, alone, began climbing a fence to enter Milton's locked stadium to practice punting.

"His efforts and commitment to football changed dramatically," Marsh said. "It just kind of lit a fire into him. He was dealing with a lot of grief, but I think he made a commitment to being the very best he could be."

Marsh knew that kind of intensity. He was an all-conference guard at Southern Mississippi, where he played with quarterback Brett Favre. But he said Jose's competitiveness was on another level. After retiring, Jose coached and played on a community men's team in a league he sponsored. Marsh played on the team, too.

"Jose always wanted to win," Marsh said, laughing.

When his parents divorced, Corliss spent summers with his father. He eventually left the Netherlands to live with Jose full time. He and his mother, Adolfine Chaar, agreed that Corliss - a gifted, highly emotional athlete with an inconsistent work ethic - could benefit from Jose's firm guidance and exacting standards.

Asked about Jose's tough-love approach when it came to athletics, Corliss smiled and offered an example. He used to run wildly around soccer fields to celebrate individually when he scored goals. Jose put a stop to that: Always celebrate with your teammates. Watch Waitman the next time he drops a punt inside the 10-yard line. The lesson stuck.

"My mom thought it would be good to have my dad more in my life to kind of push me and get me mentally more ready for what might be ahead - to kind of get the engine going," Waitman said. "It was great. He was really hard on me and helped shape me into the man I am today."

As a sophomore and junior at Milton, Waitman played both soccer and football. Jeff Klug coached him in soccer for a season and, as a football assistant, worked with him on kicking throughout high school. A former kicker who briefly played for LSU, Klug recognized that the raw punter - Waitman's warmup kicks were often shanked into the stands - had rare ability.

"It just sounded different when it came off his foot," Klug said. "Explosive. You're like, 'OK, yeah, that's not normal.'"

The problem was that Waitman's inconsistency was just as remarkable.

"He'd punt the ball 40 yards, and then shank one to the side for 10 yards," Marsh said. "Then he'd hit the next two for 45. You're like, 'Oh, my god.' Then the next three might end up in the bleachers."

Looking back, Waitman says he struggled to process his emotions that followed his father's death. At 17, however, it did provide the first sense that time was fleeting and his chances to realize his athletic potential weren't limitless. Without his dad, he also felt a responsibility to finish the work that they'd started together. And then there was his fury at life's unfairness.

"It kind of made me angry and I used some of that to just start working harder in sports, which is not necessarily a healthy thing to do," Waitman said. "But it did make me a better punter."

After Jose's death, Waitman lived with his uncle, Gaylord. He stopped playing soccer as a senior to focus on football and began working with private kicking coach Mike McCabe. That gave him the chance to train with one of McCabe's NFL clients, then-Rams punter Johnny Hekker, in nearby Pensacola and Gulf Breeze.

McCabe heard the same unusual sound. Waitman's technique needed work, but his leg had NFL potential.

"I've been doing this for 31 years," McCabe said. "And so, yeah, you can tell."

The 49ers' Corliss Waitman punts against the Washington Commanders on Oct. 19 at Levi's Stadium. (Cooper Neill/Getty Images)

At South Alabama, Waitman felt connected to his father. There were photos of Jose in the gym, and he met people who knew his dad. But Waitman's first two seasons were a nightmare. In 2014, days before his freshman season opener, he was ruled academically ineligible because some credits from the Netherlands didn't transfer. In 2015 he tore his ACL in the third game of the season.

Two years later, Waitman ranked eighth in the nation in gross punting average, at 45.2 yards, and was named first-team All-Sun Belt Conference. The determination his dad helped instill has come in handy in the NFL. Since entering the league as an undrafted free agent, Waitman has been waived nine times and made stops with six teams.

"No matter what the situation, Corliss always had a positive attitude," said former South Alabama head coach Joey Jones. "One of the reasons he's made it as far as he has is his mindset, mental toughness and wanting to be the best at what he does."

Said Klug: "How many times has he been told, 'No, you can't do it. No, you can't do it'? And he just keeps going."

What Waitman's coaches praised even more was his integrity. McCabe called him an "amazing young man of character." Said Klug: "I have an extreme love for the kid. How can you not?" Jones, South Alabama's coach for the program's first 10 seasons, said, "I'm not saying this because you're making the phone call, he's one of my favorite players I ever coached." Marsh pointed to Waitman's frequent trips back to Milton and his work in the community.

"His reputation preceded him," 49ers long snapper Jon Weeks said. "From everyone I talk to after we signed him, I mean, everyone absolutely loves him."

Waitman, a regular in the 49ers' postgame prayer huddles, credits his faith for his outlook. But he hasn't found answers to the questions that followed his father's death. Does everything happen for a reason? He's not sure why he lost his dad at 17.

"I feel that everything that's happened helped get me to here," Waitman said. "I wish some things were different, but I don't feel like every single thing that happened has to be explained. I just have to deal with it, keep pushing and trying to inspire people."

Thirteen years ago, Waitman found inspiration in the midst of his grief. He set out to honor his father, who would now be so proud, looking at the man his son has become.

This article originally published at After his father's death, 49ers' Corliss Waitman found purpose amid his pain.

#2684. Michigan Football legend goes off on Kyle Whittingham: ‘It’s bad, fellas’

It has not been a fun week for the Michigan Wolverines. Since failing to beat a 2-6 Michigan State Spartans squad, the floodgates have opened with opinions about the current state of this program. Heading across the country to Eugene to face Oregon, it's about as worse case scenario as possible from an external standpoint.

From my time in the radio business, most former players and coaches will support their respective organizations almost to the death. You've seen it throughout this series where Biff Poggi, Taylor Lewan, Jake Butt and Devin Gardner have praised Whittingham's hire and taken the positives at just about every angle.

When that starts to flip, you know things are really bad. We're beyond that point, as Butt and Gardner have already been scrutinizing the staff. Now, Lewan really let it loose this week on Bussin with The Boys, even though he said multiple times that in the pre-show that he didn't want to get into this level of conversation:

"Coach (Whittingham) looks asleep at the wheel," Lewan said. "Our head coach sat at the podium and said, 'Team looked really good a week ago (against Rutgers). Not sure what happened against Michigan State.' The game we played a week ago was Rutgers. We scored 28 points and that's the most points we have scored against any team that wasn't (UTEP). It's bad fellas.

"I saw a group of individuals for 60 minutes seem like they don't care (about beating Michigan State), and I don't think it's the kids' fault. I think the kids are a direct reflection of the leadership of that coaching staff."

Lewan shared a story of a text exchange he had with Jim Harding after it was announced he was taking over play calling for the rest of the year.

"From an offensive standpoint, there is no leadership. Nothing," he said. "I texted (Harding) last night and said, 'Buddy, I'm rootin' for ya. Anything you need from me, let me know'… (Harding replied): 'Thank you, Taylor, for the message.' What a response. It was one of those little brackets of what you could say back. #2683. FAA lifts ground stop, clearing the way for NFL teams to travel on Saturday

Friday’s sudden, and objectively concerning, decision by the FAA to issue only the second nationwide order to keep all planes from flying since 9/11 has ended.

The situation should result in no impact on NFL teams traveling to their road games for Sunday. It also should allow college teams to get to wherever they need to go for Saturday.

If it had happened one day later, the end result could have created chaos for NFL teams, significantly delaying their travel and turning their schedules for the night before the game upside down.

The situation came as a surprise to some NFL teams. For example, 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan learned about it during his Friday press conference.

Asked about the ground stop impacting the team’s plans for travel to Dallas on Saturday based on the ground stop, Shanahan said, “When did they do that?”

Eventually, Shanahan said, “I didn’t know. I just first heard.”

The 49ers plan to leave San Francisco at 1:00 p.m. PT on Saturday. Ten other teams will be traveling on Saturday, too.

#2681. ‘Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles

'Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Anfernee Simons and Jabari Walker shared the floor for 128 games in Portland. The Trail Blazers won 43 of them.

They sat beside one another in the Sixers' interview room Thursday night after a victory and discussed what the other 85 taught them.

"Whether you've got a big role or a small role, it's hard to win in the NBA," Simons said. "We've seen it firsthand."

Their roles were considerably different then.

Simons was an established starter entrusted with creating and scoring. Walker, a 2022 second-round pick, was trying to establish himself in a rotation. During their three overlapping seasons, Portland went 33-49, 21-61 and 36-46. The Blazers missed the playoffs each year.

Both are now reserves on a Sixers team constructed to contend. In nine games they've both appeared in this season, Philadelphia is 7-2.

They provided 26 points, 11 rebounds and six three-pointers in the Sixers' 123-112 win over the Raptors at Xfinity Mobile Arena. Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range. Walker recorded nine points and eight rebounds, including four on the offensive glass.

The Sixers outscored Toronto by 24 points during Simons' 23 minutes. Neither former Blazer committed a turnover.

Their production helped Philadelphia overcome a 17-point first-quarter deficit and improve to 10-3 without LeBron James.

"You learn once you come off the bench to kind of read the game before you get in there," Simons said. "Obviously, we started off kind of slow. You just want to go in, bring some energy, get some stops, get out and run. I think everybody who got off the bench brought energy."

Simons supplied an immediate lift with a deep three-pointer at the first-quarter buzzer. His shot ended an 8-0 Sixers run and trimmed Toronto's lead to nine.

He remained involved during an 11-0 burst late in the third quarter, knocking down a three and setting up Walker for a basket. Walker then made a three early in the fourth before Simons scored on the Sixers' next possession.

When Toronto pulled within six with less than five minutes remaining, Simons answered with his fifth three-pointer.

Making those shots is the most obvious way Simons can help a roster already featuring James, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown. He said the Sixers have not made him feel as though every opportunity must go in.

"They encourage us to keep shooting the ball," Simons said. "Knowing that a team has that much confidence in us to keep shooting makes the game that much easier. Whether you miss or make, as long as we get the right shots in the right moments, I think everybody can live with the misses and makes."

Simons spent seven seasons in Portland before playing last year with Boston and Chicago. His move to Philadelphia reunited him with Walker and Rayan Rupert, another former Blazer who joined the Sixers on a two-way contract during the offseason.

Knowing familiar faces awaited him helped Simons enter another new locker room.

"It made the transition seamless," he said. "Just being able to have some comfortability with guys that I played with for multiple years. It's been fun, kind of feeling like a little bit of old times. Me, Bari and Rups have been through a lot."

Walker's path to Philadelphia began a year earlier and required an additional step.

After playing 188 games over three seasons with Portland, Walker signed a two-way contract with the Sixers in July 2025. He earned a standard contract in February and has since pushed his way into the backup-center conversation despite standing 6-foot-7.

Walker believes some of the work he did on losing teams was easily missed.

"When I first got to the league, I was part of a rebuilding process," he said. "I just felt like some of the little things I did didn't always get noticed when you're losing. I told myself, if I ever got to be part of a winning organization, then I'd go out and expand my abilities."

Rebounding has made Walker difficult for Nick Nurse to overlook.

Walker credited his timing and strong hands to lessons passed down by his father, former NBA center Samaki Walker. Those instincts have become especially useful while the Sixers piece together their frontcourt behind Embiid.

"Rebounding is a skill I kind of honed in on," Walker said. "My dad was a good rebounder. He was known for his rebounding and his timing. I think it's just a gift that he transferred to me."

Walker has made it clear that he expected to earn a role this season.

"I don't know if I was delusional, but I always felt like I was going to play and I was going to be a part," he said. "I read something where they said it's a surprise, but if you were around me this summer, it wouldn't be a surprise. This is expected, and I just want to continue to get better."

The freedom Simons once had in Portland is no longer necessary. Walker does not need a high volume of touches, either. Both understand that playing beside the Sixers' stars requires shooting when open, moving the ball and handling the less glamorous work.

"You've got to find ways to impact the game multiple ways, even if you're not scoring," Simons said. "Whether it's cutting, making the right read and pass to Joel, being the right swing pass to VJ, boxing out on defense or just being in the right position."

Their opportunities will fluctuate. Simons may take nine shots one night and only a few the next. Walker's minutes will depend on matchups and the health of Philadelphia's frontcourt.

Winning has changed what they are being asked to do. Their three years together in Portland taught them why the adjustment is worthwhile.

"You feel appreciative of the times where you go into a situation where your role might be a little bit less, but you're winning," Simons said. "That's something you can't take for granted."

#2680. Scuole, allarme bomba da Roma alla Toscana: alunni portati fuori

Ad Arezzo i bambini della Tricca sono stati accompagnati al parco Pertini in attesa dei genitori.

Un allarme bomba via email ha raggiunto centinaia di scuole italiane l’11 novembre 2026. Secondo quanto riportato da Corriere, Negli istituti che hanno ricevuto la segnalazione anonima, dirigenti e personale stanno facendo uscire gli studenti in via precauzionale, per consentire le verifiche. Gli avvisi riguardano anche Roma, Frosinone e Rieti, oltre a città e province da Nord a Sud.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Nel messaggio si legge: «Ho appena lasciato nel vostro edificio, all'interno di un sacchetto di plastica, un potente ordigno esplosivo con innesco a distanza». La mail è firmata da Mikhail Andropov, che si presenta come «leader del Vilajat del Misoginistan». Si tratta del contenuto della minaccia, non di una presenza di esplosivi accertata.

Una comunicazione di allarme bomba è stata inviata via email a tutte le scuole di Roma. La polizia, contattata dagli istituti, ha indicato di liberare gli edifici con calma. Gli studenti sono tornati nelle proprie abitazioni.

Tra le province in cui risultano segnalazioni figurano anche Frosinone e Rieti. Fuori dal Lazio, gli avvisi sono stati registrati nelle province di Venezia, Trieste, Padova e Brescia, oltre che a Potenza; altre province si stanno aggiungendo all’elenco. Secondo quanto riferisce Corriere, la matrice comune delle email alimenta il sospetto che la minaccia possa essere collegata a un nuovo attacco informatico contro le istituzioni italiane. Nei giorni precedenti circa 200 presidi di scuole di ogni ordine e grado avevano già ricevuto una segnalazione simile.

In Toscana le email minatorie hanno portato a evacuazioni in più province. Tra Firenze e il suo territorio sarebbero cinque gli istituti coinvolti. Altri avvisi riguardano la provincia di Arezzo, con scuole di ogni ordine e grado, dall’infanzia alle superiori, e le province di Siena e Pisa.

Ad Arezzo città i bambini della scuola elementare Tricca sono stati accompagnati al parco Pertini in attesa dei genitori. Sono state evacuate anche la primaria di Staggiano e la scuola materna di Matrignano. Nel Casentino hanno lasciato gli edifici il liceo scientifico Galilei di Poppi e l’Itis Fermi di Bibbiena.

In Versilia, il Comune di Seravezza ha scritto su Facebook: «Una email, arrivata all'Istituto comprensivo, ha annunciato la presenza di un ordigno alla scuola primaria Frediani. Scattate quindi le procedure di evacuazione che hanno interessato sia gli alunni della scuola sia i dipendenti del Municipio».

A Modena è in corso l’evacuazione di almeno cinque istituti superiori e di una scuola primaria. La stessa misura interessa altri due istituti superiori a Vignola e Sassuolo. La polizia locale presidia le scuole coinvolte per garantire la viabilità.

#2679. At least 50 different quarterbacks will have started games through Week 10

Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza will make his first career start on Sunday. Two others will make their debuts, too: Cardinals quarterback Carson Beck and Dolphins quarterback Kyle McCord.

Via NBC Sports research, they’ll become the 48th, 49th, and 50th different quarterbacks to start games during the 2026 season.

It will be only the second time in the last 15 years (excluding the 1987 strike season) during which 50 different quarterbacks have started games in the first 10 weeks of a season.

If, for some reason, another quarterback makes his first start of the season on Sunday (that’s unlikely with Seahawks quarterback Drew Lock not having an injury designation for Sunday), it will be the second-most starters through 10 weeks since 1950.

In 1999, 55 different quarterbacks started games through the first 10 weeks of the season.

Most of the changes have arisen from injury. For the Raiders, the transition to Mendoza happened after Kirk Cousins was traded to the Vikings.

#2677. Joe Burrow can join Peyton Manning as only QBs with 4 total TDs in 5 straight games

Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow has been racking up touchdowns recently, and if he continues to do it on Sunday night against the Steelers, he’ll join some very exclusive company in NFL history.

Burrow has had at least four touchdowns, combined rushing and passing, in each of the last four games. If Burrow has another four-touchdown game on Sunday night, he will join Peyton Manning as the only quarterbacks in NFL history with at least four combined passing and rushing touchdowns in five consecutive games.

Burrow’s last four games:Three touchdown passes and one touchdown run in a 34-17 win over the Falcons.Five touchdown passes and one touchdown run in a 43-36 win over the Titans.Four touchdown passes in a 35-13 win over the Ravens.Four touchdown passes in a 31-24 win over the Dolphins.

Manning became the first quarterback to have five straight games with four touchdowns in Weeks 8-12 of 2004 with the Colts, when he had a six-touchdown game, two five-touchdown games and two four-touchdown games. (All of Manning’s touchdowns were passing, not rushing.) Manning was named NFL MVP that season.

And Burrow is an MVP candidate with the way he’s playing now. A win over the Steelers on Sunday night would put the Bengals in first place in the AFC North, and a big game with those big stakes would give a big boost to Burrow’s MVP chances.

#2676. 4 Reasons Houston Astros Fans Have to Be Thankful This Thanksgiving

As Thanksgiving approaches, Astros fans have plenty to be grateful for.

A year ago, Josh Hader was in the early stages of completing a throwing program with the intent of being ready for spring training. He'd ultimately return to action on June 3rd in a thrilling 11-9 win over the Pirates, overcoming a 5 run deficit. It would be the first save of Hader's amazing comeback. Hader would appear in 45 contests and convert all 26 of his save opportunities. Opposing clubs managed to only hit .125 against him. We can be thankful that Hader has two more guaranteed years left on his deal.

Speaking of comebacks, Hayden Wesneski returned after enduring a 15-month rehab stint from Tommy John surgery. His recovery began throwing off a mound in the Florida Complex League before steadily progressing to Double-A. On July 29th, Wesneski was activated from the injured list and earned a win in his season debut verses the Angels. His signature sweeper pitch would notch 6 wins for an Astros staff in dire need of quality starts.

The head of the table for our tribute is none other than Jose Altuve. Sitting at 2,111 regular season contests, he'll pass Jeff Bagwell next season for second place in all-time games played. As the face of the franchise, he's worth every penny of his $30 million dollar contract. A pair of championships, along with seven silver slugger awards along with 9 All-Star appearances. His most recent milestone occurred on September 9th when he notched his 2,500th career hit verses the Phillies.

Last but not least, there's Yordan Alvarez. After an injury shortened 2025 season, Alvarez would appear in a career high of 158 games. Everyone points to the massive offensive production but for me, the most remarkable stat was centered around his overall plate discipline, drawing 109 walks against only 120 strikeouts. Yordan is entering the prime of his career, set to turn just 30 years of age next June.

The Astros gave their fans plenty to be thankful for in 2026 and the table is already being set for more.

#2675. Sixers, Brown have a ‘humbling' night in loss to Celtics

Sixers, Brown have a 'humbling' night in loss to Celtics originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Whatever Jaylen Brown and the Sixers dreamed up for their first matchup against the Celtics soon flew out the window on Tuesday night.

Brown was whistled for two early fouls, the Sixers fell behind and their early-season flaws were on full display in a 123-101 loss at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

"We've just got to get better," Brown said. "Tonight was humbling. We got outplayed, out-executed. So we go back to the drawing board and get ready for the next one."

Over 26 minutes, Brown had 13 points on 4-for-9 shooting and five rebounds against the team that traded him away this summer.

As for the endless dissection of his relationship with former co-star Jayson Tatum, Brown didn't have much to add Tuesday. There was no public reconciliation, no obvious on-court animosity and generally nothing to satisfy fans hoping for some kind of fireworks on that front.

"I'm just focused on doing what's best for my team," Brown said. "Everything else … to be honest, I wasn't paying attention. But credit to Jayson; he played well tonight. Credit to the Celtics. They executed, they shot the hell out of the ball and they were the better team tonight."

Tatum scored 21 points, two of which came on a third-quarter slam over LeBron James. Paul George continued his fantastic start as a Celtic by dropping 36 points and draining six three-pointers.

The Celtics dominated from beyond the arc, shooting 22 for 49 (44.9 percent). The Sixers went just 11 for 37 (29.7 percent) on another night of underwhelming offense. The team sits 22nd in the NBA in offensive rating, 24th in three-point makes per game and 21st in three-point percentage.

"I think that we've got some guys that are obviously shooting much lower percentages than their last season or their career average — almost a handful of guys," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "And I don't think it's because they're shooting fallaway, totally contested ones. I think they're shots we want them to take. So I think they'll continue to take 'em and I'm pretty sure those will even out into their career averages."

Joel Embiid is at 37 percent from the floor and 4 for 33 from three-point range (12.1 percent).

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center got through an injury scare when he rolled his ankle late in the second quarter and hit a three early in the third. It was his first long-range make since the Sixers' home opener back on Oct. 22.

"It's a work in progress," Embiid said. "I think the biggest thing is just not thinking. I'm probably overthinking it. The rhythm of the game is different. I'm so used to having to create for myself, so it's a little bit different.

"But I think I'm slowly getting better. You could see as soon as I made a three, the next shot in the short corner … I didn't even think about it. I just shot it and let it fly, and I made it. … I think it's just about taking what's in front of you. Make or miss, keep working on your game. It's going to get there at some point."

Even with the Sixers second in the Eastern Conference standings at 9-3, Embiid believes the team's defense has "slacked off a little bit" in recent games.

"I don't really look at the record," he said. "I just look at the process of, 'Are we getting better every day?' We can always do a better job at all phases of the game."

"They're one of the top teams in the league and they've been together for a while," Brown said. "We've got a lot to work on over here, so we've got to get to work."

The Sixers will face the Raptors on Thursday night in Philadelphia.

They'll have to wait until Jan. 21 in Boston to see the Celtics again.

"I was looking forward to this," Brown said. "I was looking forward to playing well, but s— happens. Just get ready for the next one."

#2673. Saints sent Jordyn Tyson to renowned hamstring specialist at University of Wisconsin

In 2021, the NFL awarded a $4 million grant to Dr. Bryan Heiderscheit and his team at the University of Wisconsin to research new ways to prevent and treat hamstring injuries. Saints rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson may benefit from that research.

Mike Triplett of NewOrleans.Football reports that the Saints sent Tyson on two separate visits to the University of Wisconsin to be evaluated by Dr. Heiderscheit and his team.

Hamstring injuries have been a major problem for Tyson, who was out for three months with a hamstring injury before finally making his NFL debut last week. Tyson also missed time at Arizona State last year because of a hamstring injury, and he didn’t run at either Arizona State’s Pro Day or the NFL Scouting Combine because of his hamstring.

But there’s hope for Tyson after his evaluations in Wisconsin. Heiderscheit was able to identify a weakness with Tyson’s hamstring that he thinks can be strengthened with a specific workout regimen that Tyson has been following.

Heiderscheit previously worked with Packers wide receiver Christian Watson and helped him recover from hamstring injuries, and it worked: Watson has started every game this season and in nine games already has career-highs with 49 catches for 879 yards, and he’s leading the NFL with an average of 17.9 yards per catch.

That’s the kind of player the Saints think Tyson can be, if he can stay healthy. Heiderscheit’s treatment may be the key to Tyson staying healthy.

Ruthie Cecelia Foster (born February 10, 1964) is an American singer-songwriter of blues and folk music. She mixes a wide palette of American song forms, from gospel and blues to jazz, folk and soul. She has often been compared to Bonnie Raitt and Aretha Franklin. Foster has been nominated for multiple Grammy Awards for Best Blues Album and Best Contemporary Blues Album, and won her first Grammy on February 2, 2025.

Foster is from Gause, Texas, and comes from a family of gospel singers. At the age of fourteen, Foster was a soloist in her hometown choir and was certain that her future would revolve around music. After high school, she moved to Waco, Texas, and she began fronting a blues band, learning how to command a stage in the bars of Texas. Hoping to travel and gain a wider world perspective, Foster joined the United States Navy, and soon began singing in the naval band Pride which played pop and funk hits at recruitment drives.

Following her tour of duty, Foster headed to New York City where she became a regular performer at various local folk venues. Atlantic Records heard of Foster's talent and offered her a recording deal with the intent of cultivating her as a budding pop star, but Foster was not interested in a pop career. When her mother fell ill in 1993, Foster left New York and returned to Texas while she cared for her mother who died in 1996.

In 1997, Foster self-released the album Full Circle, the success of which paved the way to a long relationship with the record label Blue Corn Music. Foster's awards list includes three Grammy nominations (Let It Burn for Best Blues Album, The Truth According to Ruthie Foster for Best Contemporary Blues Album, and Promise of a Brand New Day for Best Blues Album), her numerous wins at the Blues Music Awards, including three awards for Best Female Vocalist and one for DVD of the Year for Live At Antone's, and Foster's crown for Best Female Vocalist at the 2013 Austin Music Awards. Foster earned the 2025 Grammy Award for Best Contemporary Blues Album for her album Mileage, her 13th album. She continues to tour and her shows have spanned across the U.S., Italy, Germany, Spain, and Cuba.

#2669. Fabiani, contratto in scadenza con la Lazio: “Ne parleremo a tempo debito”

Il ds parla del momento della Lazio e del contratto in scadenza: “Ne parleremo a tempo debito. Il calcio non è un semplice contratto”.

Lazio, Fabiani sul futuro: “Il calcio non è un semplice contratto”. E su Formello...

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

La Lazio è capolista della Serie A, ma risultati e classifica non rappresentano l’aspetto che rende maggiormente soddisfatto Angelo Fabiani. Il direttore sportivo biancoceleste guarda soprattutto a ciò che è stato costruito all’interno di Formello.

Intervistato da La Gazzetta dello Sport, Fabiani ha parlato del momento vissuto dalla Lazio, del lavoro portato avanti nel corso della propria carriera e anche del suo contratto in scadenza.

Proprio sul futuro il dirigente ha preferito non anticipare nulla, affidandosi però a una frase significativa: “Ne parleremo a tempo debito. Il calcio non è un semplice contratto”.

Secondo quanto riportato da La Gazzetta dello Sport, Fabiani ha spiegato cosa lo rende maggiormente felice dell’attuale momento della Lazio.

La classifica potrebbe rappresentare la risposta più immediata. Il direttore sportivo, invece, guarda oltre i risultati ottenuti sul terreno di gioco.

“Potrei dire i risultati, la classifica. Ma dove arriveremo chi lo sa. La cosa che invece mi rende felice è l’ambiente che si è creato a Formello. Il calcio è alchimia e qui è stata trovata quella giusta”.

Parole che raccontano il momento vissuto dalla Lazio capolista, ma anche l’importanza che Fabiani attribuisce alla costruzione dell’ambiente intorno alla squadra.

Un lavoro che il dirigente biancoceleste ha già affrontato diverse volte nel corso della propria carriera.

“Ho girato l’Italia in lungo e in largo, sempre per ricostruire. Alla Triestina, al Genoa, con il Messina e poi alla Salernitana, dove è iniziato il sodalizio con Lotito. Ora sto cercando di farlo alla Lazio”.

C’è però anche una questione personale ancora da affrontare. Il contratto di Fabiani è in scadenza.

Interrogato sul tema, il direttore sportivo non ha voluto accelerare i tempi né fornire indicazioni su quello che accadrà.

“Ne parleremo a tempo debito. Il calcio non è un semplice contratto”.

Una risposta breve con cui Fabiani rimanda ogni discorso sul proprio futuro. Il presente, intanto, è quello di una Lazio in testa alla Serie A e di un ambiente a Formello che il direttore sportivo considera il vero motivo di soddisfazione di questo momento.

#2668. Back in Philadelphia with Celtics, Paul George looks forward to ‘a regular game'

Back in Philadelphia with Celtics, Paul George looks forward to 'a regular game' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Paul George's presence back in town was one of the many swirling morning storylines at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

For good reason, former Celtics teammates Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum will draw immense attention Tuesday night. After all, Brown has said there "might be a little lamb chops with some gravy" between the two, if not a full-blown beef.

But George's return to Philadelphia is more than a tiny subplot. Following two seasons in Philadelphia, he was the centerpiece of the Sixers' summer trade package to acquire Brown.

George told reporters before the Celtics' shootaround that it feels like "a regular game."

"Had I been here eight, nine, 10 years, different story," he said. "I was here two years. Obviously, we didn't have the best of luck or had a great, I think, partnership in terms of my ability to stay healthy and on the floor. So that kind of played into a lot of it.

"But obviously, it's a tremendous fan base, a great sports town to play in. So that was appreciated. There's no ill will for me. It'll be fun to just compete. And outside of that, it's a normal game."

The 36-year-old George indeed had trouble staying available for sustained stretches as a Sixer. He dealt with a variety of injuries and served a 25-game suspension last season for violating the NBA's anti-drug policy.

George did play well on both ends of the floor for much of the 2026 playoffs. He helped the Sixers come back to win a seven-game first-round series against the Celtics in historic fashion. The nine-time All-Star also brought a veteran steadiness to the Sixers' locker room and was glad to mentor younger players like VJ Edgecombe.

"Just his routine … even when he got hot, he didn't try to force it," Jabari Walker said Tuesday morning. "His game was smooth and I think that's how he is as a person, just not forcing anything and having a calm energy."

George has certainly enjoyed his early days as a Celtic.

Through nine games, he's averaged 20.4 points, 5.2 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 2.3 steals while shooting 42.5 percent from three-point range. Boston will enter Tuesday night's matchup second in the Eastern Conference standings at 8-2, the Sixers first at 9-2.

"I've been kind of blown away," George said. "I think it exceeded my expectations since being in Boston. You never know how much culture is involved and how much culture changes your outlook on things and the effect it has mentally, physically, just being in an environment … and the culture that Boston presents.

"So I've been thrilled. I've been playing some of my best basketball of late, and just been enjoying grinding it out with these guys out here. It's a fun style of play and I can't talk (enough) about just the thrill, the happiness and the excitement and joy that it has brought being here."

He was asked what sort of reception he expects from Sixers fans.

"Not sure," George said. "In some ways, I helped land them a future piece for them. So with that, not sure how the reception would be."

#2666. Ground stop nudges Ole Miss-Oklahoma game to Sunday (and OU doesn't like that)

Friday’s nationwide shutdown of the aviation system has resulted in a delayed kickoff for several college football games on Saturday. One of them was moved to Sunday — and the home team isn’t happy.

The Ole Miss visit to Oklahoma shifted from 4:15 p.m. ET on Saturday to Sunday at 1:00 p.m. ET.

“The Ole Miss football team was unable to depart Oxford Friday night due to the FAA ground stoppage,” the SEC said in a statement. “After the stoppage was lifted, a late-night departure could not be accommodated by the charter company with which Ole Miss was contracted and the team’s departure has been delayed until Saturday afternoon.”

Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny strenuously objected to the decision to move the game to Sunday.

“After multiple conversations with the league office, Commissioner [Greg] Sankey informed us of his decision to move our game to Sunday, over our strong objection,” Denny said. “He further informed us that our failure to play on Sunday at the directed time would result in a forfeit. I understand that difficult decisions sometimes must be made under extraordinary circumstances. But those decisions must also consider the impact on everyone involved. Put simply, this decision isn’t fair to our athletes, our institution, or to Sooner Nation.”

Oklahoma nevertheless will comply with the decision. Even if the Sooners don’t like the decision to play the game later.

“Rescheduling the game has a significant impact, particularly on our fans,” Denny said. “Those who have made travel arrangements, accommodations, and personal plans around a Saturday game now face unnecessary disruption and hardship. Their time, commitment, and investment deserve greater consideration than they were afforded in the conference’s decision tonight. . . . We are obligated to play the game when directed. But we remain steadfast in our belief that the wrong outcome was reached this evening.”

On one hand, there’s no point huffing and puffing if Oklahoma ultimately wasn’t going to blow the house down. On the other hand, the school may have felt compelled to do something to deflect the frustrations of those who weren’t happy with having the game moved to the next day.

The bottom line is that the ground stop created travel disruptions and inconveniences for millions of people. And few are thrilled about that.

Oklahoma chose to complain. If it makes them feel better, fine. In the end, it doesn’t change the fact that the game will be added to the cluster of NFL games that begin at the same time on Sunday afternoon.

#2665. Amid a bittersweet winning streak, Rams look for revenge against Cardinals

The Rams bounced back from an embarrassing, season-opening performance and a 2-4 start.

Myles Garrett returned to the lineup and dominated.

Coach Sean McVay's team is now riding a three-game winning streak.

It took awhile, but the team that opened the season as the Super Bowl favorite is finally on a roll.

With receiver Puka Nacua the latest star to hit injured reserve, the Rams are anything but giddy heading into Sunday's game against the Arizona Cardinals in Glendale, Ariz.

"It has been unique with the amount of different information that you're dealing with and different injuries," McVay said, "but we're excited to have won those last three games."

The Rams have not lost since Oct. 18, when Cardinals coach Mike LaFleur — the Rams' former offensive coordinator — outcoached McVay in an 18-16 victory at SoFi Stadium. The Cardinals' victory extended the LaFleur brothers' record to 6-0 over McVay, who is 0-5 against Green Bay Packers coach Matt LaFleur.

The Rams subsequently defeated the Las Vegas Raiders, the Chargers and the Washington Commanders.

But tight end Terrance Ferguson suffered a hamstring injury the day before the Rams departed to play the Commanders, and Nacua suffered a knee sprain and toe injury on the Rams' final play of the 20-13 victory.

"There have been a lot of people in and out, [which] sometimes takes that major joy out of a win sometimes," quarterback Matthew Stafford said when asked about the team's mood. "You're like, 'Man, we just won, but we lost Puka for a little bit of time,' or we lost 'Ferg.' ...

"That's part of it. Then I think, frankly, there are opportunities for us to play better a little bit as well."

The Rams, who led the NFL in offense and scoring last season, are tied for fourth in yards, averaging 379.8, and 13th in points (23.8).

The defense is giving up 302.4 yards and 20.1 points per game, which ranks fifth and eighth, respectively.

Special teams problems that plagued the Rams in the first seven games appear to be resolved for now.

Rams linebacker Nate Landman tackles Cardinals running back Tyler Allgeier on Oct. 18 at SoFi Stadium. (Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times)

Last season, after Davante Adams suffered a hamstring injury, McVay masterfully pivoted to an attack relying heavily on multiple tight ends.

With Nacua and Adams out, will McVay make another significant shift? Perhaps a two-back set?

"I think you explore everything," McVay said.

Running backs Kyren Williams and Blake Corum said they can carry a heavier load and also augment a depleted receiver corps that now includes Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell, Xavier Smith, Brennan Presley and rookie CJ Daniels.

"Kyren and I prepare for anything," Corum said. "Our mindset, whether we run a lot or don't, we're ready for whatever coach feels is best for this team."

Williams said he attended college recruiting camps as a slot receiver. So if McVay asked him to split out wide?

"I'm fine with it," he said. "I'll do anything with a smile on my face, especially that."

Read more: With NFL's toughest schedule looming, Rams quiet at trade deadline as rivals make deals

The last time they played the Cardinals, the Rams were without left tackle Alaric Jackson, who had been suspended for punching a Buffalo Bills player after a defeat. David Quessenberry played well in Jackson's absence, but Cardinals defensive coordinator Nick Rallis had his players blitzing throughout the game, and Stafford sustained multiple violent hits.

With Adams and Nacua sidelined, the Rams are preparing for another onslaught of pressure.

"That's been part of their M.O.," McVay said. "It's not necessarily anything that surprised us, but they do a good job. ... Protecting Matthew will always be at a premium and at the forefront of our minds, regardless of whether you have two of those premier players or not."

A victory over the Cardinals would keep the Rams on track for a possible playoff run. A defeat, with what is regarded as the league's toughest remaining schedule ahead of them, could face-plant those chances before the Rams reach their bye.

#2664. Warriors vs. Spurs player grades: LJ Cryer shines, Yaxel Lendeborg struggles

Well, that was not a fun game at all. The Golden State Warriors lost 123-85 against the San Antonio Spurs, in a game that was truly over before the Dubs even scored a point. They trailed 18-0 at the halfway mark of the first quarter, and with no Steph Curry to save them, there was never a chance on the road against a team that entered the night with a 10-game winning streak.

No one needs to spend much more time thinking about this game, so let's run through the grades very, very quickly. As always, grades are based on my expectations for each individual player, with a "B" grade representing the average performance for that player.

Note: True-shooting percentage (TS) is a scoring efficiency metric that accounts for threes and free throws. Entering Friday's games, league-average TS was 57.4%.

18 minutes, 8 points, 4 rebounds, 3 assists, 1 steal, 1 block, 1 foul, 3-for-11 shooting, 2-for-6 threes, 36.4% TS, -29

Melton got the start in Curry's absence, as I'm guessing he'll continue to do. He did some good things, but also some bad things. His inability to penetrate San Antonio's defense made it hard for him to quarterback the offense, and while he had some nice defensive plays, he struggled with the Spurs' speed and length.

24 minutes, 3 points, 7 rebounds, 1 assist, 1 block, 3 turnovers, 3 fouls, 1-for-13 shooting, 0-for-2 threes, 1-for-2 free throws, 10.8% TS, -40

Well, there's no way to sugarcoat this one, other than to say the obvious: these games happen to rookies, and they're just part of the learning process. Lendeborg will get better because of this game, but he sure won't have a fun time looking back through the film.

This was a double whammy for the Dubs' first-round pick. It was his first game since he was handed the keys following Curry's injury, and it was his first time facing a team like the Spurs. They don't make players like Victor Wembanyama in the Big 10, and they don't make defenses this long, fast, or rangy. Lendeborg was at a total loss when having to deal with those things, though credit to him for not slumping his shoulders, and still playing hard on defense and on the glass.

Grade: D-Post-game bonus: Led the team in rebounds; worst plus/minus on the team.

16 minutes, 4 points, 3 rebounds, 3 assists, 1 steal, 2 turnovers, 3 fouls, 2-for-5 shooting, 0-for-2 threes, 40.0% TS, -23

Green always feels like a barometer for whether or not the team can win. You can tell by his effort level whether it's a winnable game for the Dubs. He came out energized on the first few possessions, while defending Wembanyama, and then it became clear that the Warriors had no chance and Green's effort level waned with that. Can't really blame him.

22 minutes, 8 points, 3 rebounds, 1 block, 2-for-10 shooting, 2-for-5 threes, 2-for-2 free throws, 36.8% TS, -24

With Curry out for a few weeks at a minimum, the Warriors are going to turn to Lendeborg and Podziemski to be the first options on offense. Unfortunately, the first game post-Curry's injury was a bit of a dud in that regard. Podz didn't struggle as much as Lendeborg, but it was a very forgettable game for him, as he just couldn't find any spacing against San Antonio's length, and seemed uncomfortable all night. Props to him for not turning the ball over, though.

30 minutes, 7 points, 4 rebounds, 1 assist, 2 turnovers, 4 fouls, 2-for-4 shooting, 1-for-2 threes, 2-for-2 free throws, 71.7% TS, -27

You have to give Richard so much credit for being out there and playing heavy minutes despite his thumb injury. I thought he'd be out a few months, and instead he missed a single game. He also was not the problem for Golden State in this game, though perhaps he wasn't the solution, either. He was competitive, which is more than some of his teammates could say, and he fought hard on defense while making a few things happen on offense. It was the kind of performance that stands out when you win, but showed some limitations because they lost.

24 minutes, 20 points, 2 rebounds, 6 assists, 1 steal, 1 foul, 7-for-17 shooting, 6-for-11 threes, 58.8% TS, -11

Cryer was, without a doubt, the brightest part of the game for the Warriors. Maybe the only bright part of the game, for that matter. With Curry and Brandon Williams injured, Cryer — who is on a two-way contract — is going to get some run.

He looked the part in this game. He was part of the first group of subs, and immediately started doing what his teammates had been unable to do: penetrate the defense. Like all the Dubs, he struggled to score once he did that … despite shooting better than 50% from distance, he went just 1-for-6 inside the arc.

The 20 points was a career best for Cryer, and a reminder of what he's capable of with the ball in his hands. The Warriors will need him over the next few weeks.

Grade: APost-game bonus: Led the team in points and assists.

10 minutes, 0 points, 3 rebounds, 1 assist, 0-for-2 shooting, 0-for-1 threes, 0.0% TS, 0 +/-

Horford didn't play much. Once it was clear that the Warriors were going to lose, there was no point in putting more miles on the odometer of the team's oldest player. He was fine in his minutes, though.

15 minutes, 5 points, 3 rebounds, 2 assists, 1 foul, 2-for-4 shooting, 1-for-2 threes, 62.5% TS, -15

Niang did some good things. He didn't do any great things, but he did some good things, and he didn't do any awful things, either. Just not quite athletic enough given San Antonio's players, and I thought his defense had a rough go of it.

21 minutes, 7 points, 4 rebounds, 1 assist, 1 block, 1 turnover, 1 foul, 3-for-8 shooting, 1-for-3 threes, 0-for-1 free throws, 41.5% TS, -7

He was making plays happen through sheer effort, and didn't seem quite as bothered by San Antonio's length as some of his teammates, though he still didn't have an efficient scoring night. Bassey's impressive play continued. On a night where the Warriors shot just 33.3% from the field, Bassey was the only player on the team to make more than half of his shots. He had some impressive rebounds as well. It wasn't all good, though, as San Antonio's size really got the better of him on numerous occasions. He struggled to contain anyone on defense, and the three turnovers and four fouls in the box score pretty accurately reflect how he played. But still: an efficient 11-and-5 in 20 minutes from the center position is something the Warriors are happy about.

Single-game individual plus/minus is perhaps the noisiest stat in basketball, but it still feels noteworthy — if not meaningful — that Payton was the only Warriors player to have a positive plus/minus in a game that they lost by 38 points. That's more a reflection of when he was on the court than of what he did on it, but still … worth noting!

Still, with the exception of a bunch of missed shots, Ike played fairly well. He passes really well for his position, and the game doesn't move too quickly for him. Did some nice things on defense as well.

#2663. Malik Beasley Sells Signed NBA Jerseys on TikTok Weeks Before Guilty Plea in Gambling Case

Malik Beasley opened up his collection of NBA jerseys to TikTok viewers on Wednesday night, offering memorabilia from his playing career for sale. The former Detroit Pistons guard fielded questions while holding up uniforms, including pieces from his early years with the Denver Nuggets.

The November 11 livestream came as the 29-year-old prepares to plead guilty in a federal sports betting case. His attorney, Steve Haney, confirmed the agreement on October 27, with a court appearance still ahead.

Basketball accounts including NBACentral and MrBuckBuckNBA circulated clips the following day. The footage drew attention to keepsakes from a career that spanned nine NBA seasons and six teams.

Beasley has not explained in the circulated footage whether the sale is connected to legal bills or other expenses. The recordings offer no reliable picture of his current finances or how much money he received.

Wearing a Denver uniform himself, Beasley told viewers he would personalize the items they bought. "Once you get it I will sign them myself and put your name on it," he said, according to Complex. The Nuggets selected him with the 19th overall pick in the 2016 NBA Draft.

He was less willing to part with a Minnesota Timberwolves jersey. When a viewer asked about one, Beasley acknowledged that he had it but said he wanted to keep it.

He joined Minnesota in a February 2020 trade and spent parts of three seasons there, averaging 19.6 points across 37 games in 2020-21. Minnesota traded him to the Utah Jazz in July 2022, followed by stops with the Los Angeles Lakers and Milwaukee Bucks before Detroit.

Beasley's change-of-plea hearing is scheduled for December 9 in Brooklyn federal court, Bloomberg reported. He initially pleaded not guilty on July 1, according to the Los Angeles Times.

An indictment unsealed June 29 named five other defendants, including former NBA forward Ed Davis and player agent Paolo Zamorano. The charges included wire fraud conspiracy, bribery in sporting contests, honest services wire fraud conspiracy and money laundering conspiracy.

According to the Justice Department, Beasley agreed to manipulate selected statistics while playing for Milwaukee during the 2023-24 season. Prosecutors allege that Davis passed advance information about his intended performance to others, enabling them to place bets tied to those statistics.

The indictment identified four games involving Cleveland, Charlotte, the Clippers and Brooklyn. For the February 27, 2024, Charlotte game, prosecutors described a plan to score fewer points while collecting more rebounds than the relevant betting lines anticipated. They said Beasley's compensation typically took the form of reductions or payments toward gambling debts he owed Davis.

Beasley's most recent NBA season had made him a significant contributor to Detroit's offense. He played all 82 regular-season games in 2024-25 and averaged 16.3 points, helping the Pistons return to the playoffs for the first time since 2019.

His 319 three-pointers set a franchise record, as the Pistons noted in their season review. He finished second in Sixth Man of the Year voting behind Boston's Payton Pritchard.

Detroit was discussing a three-year, $42 million contract with Beasley when the federal investigation became public in June 2025. Those negotiations were put on hold, Local 4 reported. The proposed agreement was never completed.

#2661. Future Broncos: 3 Prospects to Watch in Week 11 of NCAA Football Season

Welcome back to another installment of Future Broncos. Last week, I focused on a trio of defenders for Broncos Country to keep their eye on as the rest of the collegiate football season transpires. This week, I'll switch gears and offer three players on offense since that side of the ball has been Denver's biggest issue in 2026.

So far this season, I've offered my thoughts on a handful of offensive line prospects. Mizzou's Cayden Green, Indiana's Carter Smith, Minnesota's Greg Johnson, and USC's Elijah Paige. Based on the comments section, identifying more big guys in the offensive trenches is something you are all interested in.

Georgia fifth-year senior Earnest Green III has been on my radar for a while. Back in 2023, he was a fourteen-game starter for the Bulldogs at left tackle protecting future top pick Carson Beck. He continued to man down that position for nine games in 2024, but a lingering shoulder issue cost him a few games and slowed the promise he showed as a freshman.

Last season, Greene (6'4″, 320 pounds) flipped to right tackle while Monroe Freeling was manning the blindside. However, he started just nine games due to lingering back issues. Though he didn't give up a sack in the over 800 offensive snaps he played in 2005.

Now healthy, Greene is back home where it all started on the left side of Georgia's stalwart offensive line. The redshirt senior is poised to finish his collegiate career with over 40 starts and over 3,000 snaps between both tackle positions and having three different line coaches. That experience will pay off and mean a lot to NFL scouts and general managers who value experience and top-notch SEC pedigrees.

I'm a big fan of the depth he gets in his pass sets. I also like his ability to anchor and hold his own against strong power rushers. Moreover, I am impressed with his ability to get up field and take on blockers at the second level. It'll be interesting to see how he measures [arm length] during the pre-draft circuit. There are some who believe his best football is inside at guard, but I think he can stick at tackle.

Last week's performance versus Ole Miss earned him the Outland Trophy Player of the Week honors. To date, Greene has only given up four quarterback pressures on the season. The Broncos could use a tough and battle-tested player in their trenches next April, and I believe Greene (if medicals check out) has a shot at being a Day 2 selection. You can catch him in action this afternoon on ABC when the top-ranked Bulldogs host Mizzou.

For most of my Future Broncos installments, I've tried to focus on seniors whether it be fourth or fifth-year players. One particular reason is that NIL money has changed the NFL Draft landscape. Early declarations are basically half of what they used to be. In turn, that makes it a lot harder to find quality players to address needs.

However, a potential early round pick that may wind up declaring early if he keeps playing well is Notre Dame offensive lineman Anthonie Knapp. He manned down the left tackle position for the Fighting Irish for the first 27 games of his collegiate career. For his third season, the junior has kicked inside to guard.

That's where many analysts have stated his best NFL potential might be. However, there are a handful of others who think a further kick inside to the pivot may be where he blossoms. Regardless, his versatility will be a big enhancer for his draft stock if he chooses to declare.

We all know Head Coach Sean Payton values experience and versatility when it comes to offensive lineman. This Golden Domer certainly fits the bill. By the end of this season, Knapp (6'5", 305 pounds) will have logged well over 2,000 snaps and have three full seasons of starting experience.

While he could stand to put on some weight and muscle to handle the rigors of the pro game, his anchor is incredibly strong at this stage. In my opinion, he plays with NFL ready technique at the line of scrimmage. He has been an enforcer in the run game and a key reason for Notre Dame's success on the ground this season. As a pass protector, Knapp has been credited with giving up just one sack in nearly three dozen starts.

Whether or not Knapp chooses to declare remains to be seen but given Denver's long-term needs at multiple positions on the offensive line, he would be a quality prospect for them to consider. I believe he has a legitimate shot to be a Top 50 player easily if he decides to take his talents to the NFL. You can watch him in action when the third-ranked Fighting Irish host Boston College this afternoon.

Thus far in our Future Broncos installments, we have highlighted just two tight ends in the 2027 NFL Draft. Underclassmen Oregon's Jamari Johnson and Virginia Tech's Luke Reynolds. I have a strong feeling both of them will declare and will merit early consideration by NFL teams looking to upgrade the position.

This collegiate season, another underclassman from Iowa is making quite the statement this season—DJ Vonnahme. Over the years, the Hawkeyes have been a tight end producing factory under Kirk Ferentz. Players like George Kittle, Noah Fant, T.J. Hockensen, and Sam LaPorta all come to mind.

Vonnahme (6'4", 241 pounds) appears to be next to follow in their footsteps. Appearing in twelve games as a redshirt freshman in 2025, Vonnahme logged five starts and was the Hawkeyes' leading receiver with 29 catches, 434 yards, and 3 touchdowns. He popped onto the map of scouts last season with a dominant seven catch, 146-yard performance against Vanderbilt in last year's ReliaQuest Bowl.

In eight games in 2026, Vonnahme sports 32 receptions for 314 yards and 3 touchdowns as well as one rushing touchdown. His yards per route ran (2.59) is amongst the highest in the nation. He has one of the best contested catch rates in the nation and can work multiple levels of the field.

While there is no doubting his upside and talent as a receiving threat at the next level, Vonnahme's work as a blocker leaves a lot to be desired. It's important to note he is only 20 years old and is a former quarterback that is still learning the nuances of the position. Getting better at blocking is something he can certainly get better at with more time.

Vonnahme is just a redshirt sophomore. With that in mind, a return back to Iowa seems quite likely. Though with this year's class not having a clear-cut number one just yet, perhaps he goes pro if he gets good enough feedback in the pre-draft process. You can catch him in tonight when the sixteenth ranked Hawkeyes host Purdue tomorrow evening on NBC.
